articles.title: We Need to Talk About How Gross Modern Web Design Has Become (And How We Built an AI to Catch It)
articles.description: Let me paint a picture I know you’ve experienced recently.  You’re trying to book a flight, buy...
articles.body_html:
Let me paint a picture I know you’ve experienced recently.

You’re trying to book a flight, buy concert tickets, or just download a simple PDF converter. Suddenly, the website turns into an absolute warzone:

🚨 "ONLY 2 SEATS LEFT AT THIS PRICE!"
⏳ A blood-red countdown timer ticks down from 05:00.
🟢 Three massive, glowing "DOWNLOAD NOW" buttons appear, and you know two of them will install malware.
🥺 And when you try to close the popup? The only button says, "No thanks, I'd rather pay full price and be miserable."

We call this "marketing." But let’s be honest: it’s just deceptive engineering.

These are Dark Patterns—UI/UX choices intentionally designed to trick, guilt, or force you into doing things you didn't want to do. And honestly? It’s getting gross. As developers, we build the web. We shouldn't be okay with the web actively manipulating its users.

So, my team at Tarkash Labs decided to fight back. We built a cognitive visual shield to catch these patterns in real-time.

Meet OmniGuard AI.


(Watch the 1-minute demo above to see it catch fake timers and hidden fees live!)

🛡️ How OmniGuard Works (The Tech Stack)

The problem with most ad-blockers or privacy extensions is that they rely on static blocklists or CSS selectors. But modern dark patterns are dynamic. They are disguised as regular DOM elements.

To catch them, we needed a tool that could see the web exactly how a human sees it.

We built OmniGuard as a Manifest V3 Chrome Extension powered by a FastAPI backend and Gemini 3.7 Flash.

Here is the exact flow:

1. The "Eyes" (React 18 + Vite Extension):
When you click "Scan" (or enable auto-scan on scroll), the extension captures an ephemeral, highly compressed screenshot of your active viewport.

2. The "Brain" (FastAPI + Gemini 3.7 Flash):
The image is sent to our stateless FastAPI backend. We use Gemini 3.7 Flash’s multimodal capabilities to analyze the visual context of the page. It doesn't just read the code; it understands how the UI looks.

3. The "Shield" (Shadow DOM Injection):
If Gemini detects a dark pattern, the backend streams the exact coordinates back to the extension. We then inject a Shadow DOM layer over the page, drawing glowing red bounding boxes precisely over the deceptive elements—completely isolating our CSS from the host page's styles.

🕵️‍♂️ The 6 Villains We Hunt

OmniGuard is currently configured to detect six specific categories of visual deception. Here is how it catches them in the wild:

1. Disguised Clicks
Buttons masquerading as something else (like fake downloads that lead to ads or malware).

2. Confirmshaming
Guilt-loaded opt-out language designed to make you feel bad for not subscribing.

3. Urgency Traps
Fake countdowns and artificial scarcity messages.

4. Hidden Costs (Drip Pricing)
Fees and excluded taxes that magically appear at the very end of a checkout journey.

5. Sneak into Basket
Unwanted software bundles or insurances silently pre-checked during a download or checkout.

6. Forced Continuity
"Free trials" that hide their aggressive auto-renewal terms in the fine print.

🔒 Zero-DB Privacy Architecture

One of the biggest challenges of building an AI extension that takes screenshots of your browser is privacy. We knew from day one that if we were building a tool to protect users, we couldn't compromise their data to do it.

That’s why the OmniGuard backend is 100% stateless. It uses a zero-DB architecture. The viewport screenshot exists only in memory for the milliseconds it takes Gemini to process it, and is then immediately destroyed. Nothing is ever saved, logged, or stored.

💻 Try It Yourself (Open Source)

We’ve open-sourced the entire project. If you want to see how we handled Manifest V3 tab capturing, or how we prompted Gemini Flash for UI coordinate mapping, you can check out the repo here:

Tarkash-Labs / OmniGuard

OmniGuard is a real-time, multimodal browser extension acting as a cognitive visual shield against deceptive UI/UX. Powered by Gemini , it instantly detects "Dark Patterns"—like fake timers or hidden costs—and injects HTML5 Canvas bounding boxes to protect users before they click. Built on a secure, zero-DB privacy architecture.

🛡️ OmniGuard AI

Real-Time Multimodal Dark Pattern & Visual Deception Radar

OmniGuard AI is a Chrome browser extension that acts as a cognitive visual shield against deceptive UI/UX. Powered by Gemini 3.7 Flash, it captures what users actually see on a webpage, detects dark patterns in real-time, and overlays live bounding boxes directly on the deceptive elements — before users can click.

Built by Tarkash Labs

✨ Features

OmniGuard detects 6 categories of dark patterns in real-time:

Category Description Example
⏰ Urgency Traps Fake countdowns & artificial scarcity "Only 2 left! Order in 03:22!"
🎭 Disguised Clicks Buttons masquerading as something else Fake download buttons, hidden ads
🛒 Sneak into Basket Unwanted items silently added Pre-checked insurance add-ons
🔄 Forced Continuity Subscription traps & hidden renewals Free trial → auto-charge
😢 Confirmshaming Guilt-loaded opt-out language "No thanks, I hate saving money"
💰 Hidden Costs Fees revealed late in the
…
View on GitHub

Massive shoutout to my teammates Yug Vasava (Lead Dev) and Avadh Vaishnani (Lead QA) for helping bring this to life.

👇 Now, I need to know...

We are constantly trying to improve the AI's detection capabilities.

What is the most unethical, infuriating, or downright gross dark pattern you’ve seen a company use recently?

Drop it in the comments below so we can train OmniGuard to catch it! 🚀

articles.title: My open source project is brand new and already has contributors. Here's what I did.
articles.description: In the spirit of Hacktoberfest, with it being the last day of October, I wanted to share my story...
articles.body_html:
In the spirit of Hacktoberfest, with it being the last day of October, I wanted to share my story about open source and building in public.

I'm a DevRel. In my day job, I help people who've never contributed to open source get their first code shipped. So when I started building answerLoops, an open source, self-hostable AI support tool, one thing bugged me. Was my own project actually easy to jump into?

What is answerLoops?

answerLoops turns your knowledge source into answers for your community. It's self-hostable, so you can run it on your own infrastructure with the AI provider you choose, or use the hosted app.

Here's the workflow:

  1. A question comes in from a community channel like Discord, Slack, Discourse, GitHub, or website chat.
  2. answerLoops searches your knowledge: your docs, files, GitHub repos, and Notion pages.
  3. It drafts a reply with the sources attached.
  4. A second AI agent checks the draft against those sources.
  5. Your team approves the reply, or you turn on auto-reply for the questions that pass the check.
  6. Useful resolutions are saved as knowledge, and knowledge gaps show what your docs are missing.

That workflow is why the labels below make sense. frontend work touches the dashboard where a team reviews and approves replies. backend work touches the pipeline and the channel integrations behind it.

Explore answerLoops on ⭐️ GitHub

The project is new, so the hard part right now is getting off the ground and getting people to find it. I posted about it on Reddit and X. It didn't bring in many stars. So I changed where I put my effort. Instead of trying to reach everyone, I focused on developers who want to build something and on making it easy for them to start.

Over the last week, developers started showing up. They sent pull requests, and I merged them. Some built something from an open issue. Others found a problem on their own and fixed it.

I can't prove any of this is cause and effect. I have a handful of data points, and some of them didn't pick up an issue at all. But I did set a few things up beforehand, and I think they're worth writing down for anyone starting out.

1. I labeled issues by skill, not just by type

At first my issues only had the usual labels: enhancement, bug, documentation. That tells a contributor what kind of change it is, but not whether it's for them.

I added two labels: frontend and backend. Right now I have 58 open issues, 41 tagged frontend and 33 tagged backend. Someone can click one label and see only the work that matches their skills, without reading all 58.

I also use good first issue and help wanted. good first issue is the one most people already know. The skill labels are the new part.

Most of the PRs I merged closed an issue with one of these labels, so they look like they're doing something. I'm still careful about how much I claim.

One side effect: only 8 good first issue tickets are open now. Labels only work while there's something behind them, so I'm writing more.

2. I wrote issues like specs

I'd have undersold this one if I'd only written about labels.

The issue my first contributor picked up was tagged frontend, good first issue, and help wanted. It was also written so that someone who had never seen the codebase could start. It had:

  • A Problem section: the data was already being collected and stored, but nothing in the UI showed it.
  • A Scope section: exactly what to show, where to start looking in the code, and what the wording should be.
  • A Not in this issue section: what to leave alone, so nobody drifts into a bigger project.
  • Acceptance criteria as a checklist.

It also said it was part of a larger tracking issue, so a contributor could see where it fit.

A vague issue like "show usage on the article page" leaves a newcomer guessing about scope, wording, and what "done" means. A scoped one lets them start. If I had to pick one thing to copy, it's this.

Every issue also ends with a link to the contributing guide, and it's now built into the Issues template.

3. I made the project easy to run

You can't contribute to something you can't start. I rewrote the README to be a short overview, and added a CONTRIBUTING guide plus issue forms for bugs, features, integrations, and docs, so new reports come in with the details I need.

The first version of the setup steps wasn't good enough. It ran the Docker path, then said "or run it natively," and I couldn't tell you which one to pick. If I was confused, a newcomer was too. I rewrote it as three steps: clone the app, set the values in one .env, and run it. Then I ran the native steps myself against a fresh database to make sure they work.

Contributors have already improved the docs from there, including a diagram of the install flow in the self-hosting quickstart.

4. Review was fast, and the PRs made it easy

The PRs came with a clear description of what changed, why, and how to try it. That made them easy to review, and I could merge quickly.

Fast feedback matters. A first-time contributor who waits two weeks for a reply rarely comes back.

5. I said thank you in public

The contributors are credited in the release notes and in the docs, and I thanked them publicly. Open source is mostly volunteers, so it's the least I can do. It also shows the next person what happens when they contribute.

I also posted on LinkedIn and X.

Thanks Aaqibhafeez Khan for the kind words

What I got wrong, or am not sure of

  • I don't know if the labels worked 100%. Nothing else about the project changed much, but I also posted about it in a few places, which brings people in on its own.
  • Not everyone took a labeled issue. Some contributors found a problem nobody had filed, and the labels can't explain that.
  • Return visits are the real test. What matters is whether people come back for a second PR.
  • The supply runs out. Contributors finish good first issue tickets quickly. Writing good ones is now a regular chore for me.

If you want to try this

  • Label issues by the skill needed, not just the type of change.
  • Write one issue as a spec: problem, scope, what's out of scope, and acceptance criteria.
  • Make sure someone can run the project, and test those steps yourself.
  • Review fast.
  • Thank people in public.

If you're new to open source and want help with a first PR, leave a comment or message me. I'm happy to walk you through it. The open issues are here: https://github.com/answerLoops/answerLoops/issues

And if you maintain a project: what got your first outside contributors to show up?

P.S. If you're reading this, starring ⭐️ the repo also really helps people find it :)

Thanks for reading!

articles.title: I Built 101 Indian Monuments in the Browser Using Only Code (No 3D Models)
articles.description: There isn't a single 3D model file on this site. Every one of these 101 monuments, from the Taj...
articles.body_html:
There isn't a single 3D model file on this site. Every one of these 101 monuments, from the Taj Mahal to a Himalayan monastery, is a small JavaScript function that builds the building out of boxes, cylinders and domes.

👉 Try it: monuments-of-india-nu.vercel.app ·
Code: github.com/amananandrai/monuments-of-india

The project in numbers

  • 🏛️ 101 monuments across 26 states and union territories
  • 📦 0 downloaded 3D models, 0 build steps, 0 npm dependencies for the site
  • 🪶 ~2 KB of code per monument on average (the smallest is under 1 KB)
  • 🎨 1 shader that paints stone, brick, marble and water on all of them
  • 🌙 Day and night modes, with floodlights, festival lights and stars

Why I built it

Most people can find the Taj Mahal on a map. Far fewer could place Rani ki Vav, Ramappa or Key Monastery. I wanted a way to see how widely India's architecture is spread, and to explore each building from every angle instead of scrolling through photos.

So the site opens on a map of India, not a list. Every monument is a pin, coloured by kind: 51 temples and shrines, 25 tombs and memorials, 17 forts and palaces, and 8 civic and engineering works. Click one, and the map gives way to a 3D model you can spin, zoom and step through with the arrow keys.

Every monument also has its own link, so #taj-mahal opens the Taj directly.

How a monument is born, in five steps

Step 1: Snap together simple shapes 🧱

Think of LEGO. Instead of downloading a ready-made Qutub Minar, the code stacks simple pieces: a flat box for the base, five tapering cylinders for the storeys, a ring of balconies, and a small domed pavilion on top.

Two tricks make the shapes richer than plain LEGO:

  • Lathe works like a potter's wheel. Draw half the outline of a dome, spin it, and you get the whole dome. Every onion dome on the site comes from one shared outline.
  • Extrude works like a cookie cutter pushed through dough. Draw a flat shape, such as an arch or a star-shaped platform, and the code pushes it into a thick 3D slab.

Step 2: Crimp the edges ✨

The Qutub Minar's storeys aren't smooth tubes; they have ridges (flutes). To make them, the code walks around each cylinder and pushes the wall in and out in a wave, like crimping the edge of a pie crust. Change the wave and you get a different storey: rounded flutes at the bottom, star-shaped ones higher up.

Here's the heart of it, trimmed down:

// For every point on the tier's surface...
const a = Math.atan2(z, x);                      // how far around the tower are we?
const f = 1 + 0.07 * Math.abs(Math.cos(a * 12)); // push out in 12 waves
pos.setX(k, x * f);
pos.setZ(k, z * f);

Step 3: Reuse the small pieces 🔁

Indian architecture repeats its vocabulary: chhatris (small domed pavilions), minarets, kalash finials, shikhara spires and gopuram gateways appear again and again. These all live in one shared file, js/helpers.js, so a new monument mostly combines pieces that already exist.

This is why some monuments are tiny. The whole Somnath Temple, including the sea behind it and the arrow pillar on its sea wall, is under 1 KB, because a single helper call builds the entire temple:

nagaraTemple({ w: 14, h: 26, m: STONE, shade: SHADE, plinth: 3, urus: 8,
               halls: [[18, 9, 6], [16, 8, 5]] })

Step 4: Paint it with a "magic stone" shader 🎨

Plain shapes still look like plain shapes. What makes them read as stone is the surface shader in js/surface.js, and it's the single most important idea in the project.

The problem: normally, to put a pattern on a 3D shape you "unwrap" it, like cutting gift-wrap to fit each box by hand. Doing that for every piece of 101 buildings was never going to happen.

The solution: the pattern lives in space itself. Imagine carving each building out of one giant block of marble whose veins already run through it. Wherever you cut, the pattern is there and fits perfectly. So a one-metre block is exactly the same size on the Qutub Minar as on the walls of Agra Fort, no matter how either was built.

From that one idea, the shader draws:

  • Block joints, brick courses and marble veins. Each material is tagged with a kind (masonry, marble, brick, rock, jali screen, glazed tiles, carved frieze and more).
  • Fake bumps. It shades the joints and veins with light-and-shadow hints, the way an artist shades a pencil drawing, so flat walls look grooved.
  • Weathering. Darker grime near the ground and faint rain streaks down the walls, like a film crew aging a set.
  • A tiny random tint per piece, so a row of twenty identical columns doesn't look photocopied.
  • Moving water. Four layers of gentle, drifting ripples break up the sky's reflection, the way it looks on a real pond.

For the ten best-known monuments, the shader adds grain from real photographs (free CC0 textures from Poly Haven). Picture three projectors shining a photo of real marble onto the model from the front, the side and the top. The photo's own colour is removed and only its grain is kept, then tinted to the model's colour. The Taj stays white, the Red Fort stays red, and any other monument using the same stone gets the detail for free.

Step 5: Light it like a photograph ☀️

  • A sun with soft shadows and a sky light that gently fills the shaded side.
  • A reflection of the sky for gold, bronze and polished marble to shine with.
  • Ambient occlusion darkens corners and the undersides of roofs, where light struggles to reach, like dust settling in corners.
  • Tone mapping is the camera's exposure setting, so a bright sky doesn't turn pure white.
  • Night mode switches on floodlights and festival lights, adds a soft glow (bloom) around them, and fills the sky with stars.

None of these effects is special on its own. Stacked together, they stop your eye from reading the models as boxes.

Why code instead of 3D scans?

A 3D scan is like a photo of a cake: very detailed, but megabytes per monument, with licensing questions attached. A coded model is like the recipe: a couple of kilobytes, readable by anyone, and easy to change.

Each monument also gets a "library card" in js/data.js with its name, local-script name, coordinates, dates, style, material and the recipe that builds it:

{ id: 'taj-mahal', state: 'Uttar Pradesh', lat: 27.1751, lng: 78.0421,
  type: 'memorial', name: 'Taj Mahal', local: 'ताज महल',
  built: '1632–1653', style: 'Mughal', material: 'White Makrana marble',
  build: buildTaj }

Adding the 102nd monument means writing one module and one card. That's it.

The problems I didn't expect 🐛

1. Flickering walls. When two surfaces sit in exactly the same spot (a marble band flush with a wall, the stacked slices of a temple spire), the graphics card can't decide which one is in front, so they flicker as the camera moves, like two stickers fighting over the same place. js/coplanar.js finds every clash and nudges one surface a hair forward in depth. The shapes themselves don't change.

2. Buildings on square islands. Lawns and pavements are flat boxes, so every monument looked like it was sitting on a tile with hard edges. js/landscape.js fades their open edges into the land around them, and lets seas and long rivers run on to the horizon.

3. Hills that bent temples. Rocks, hills and trees start as rough low-poly blobs. js/naturalize.js rebuilds them in more detail and roughens them with noise, like squishing clay. The first catch: a temple sitting on a hilltop got warped along with the hill. The fix was to let hills only bulge outward, so their flat tops stay flat.

4. The ocean that shimmered. A sea made of a few giant triangles loses precision far from the camera and starts to shimmer. The water is now split into tiles, at most 60 a side.

5. Phones. Ambient occlusion and water reflections are skipped on phones to keep the frame rate smooth.

Small tools, no tooling

The whole site is index.html, one stylesheet and plain ES modules, with three.js loaded from a CDN through an import map. There's no build step, no bundler and no framework, so deploying is just pushing to main on Vercel.

Looking back, this is what kept the project moving. With no dependencies to update and no build to break, every hour went into the monuments themselves.

The map isn't a tile service either. India's outline and state borders come from Natural Earth's public-domain data, simplified into SVG paths. When you pick a monument, the camera behaves like a photographer stepping back until the whole building fits in the frame, then glides there in about a second.

10 favourites, and how they were built

  1. Konark Sun Temple, Odisha. The temple is a stone chariot for the Sun god, and its 24 carved wheels work as sundials. The model rebuilds the chariot plinth on all 24 wheels from one shared wheel() helper.
  2. Hawa Mahal, Jaipur. 953 small windows let the women of the court watch the street unseen. The latticed jali holes are cut by the shader rather than modelled, so the stone stays solid and the screens still cast the right shadows.
  3. Rani ki Vav, Gujarat. A stepwell that descends seven levels. The ground is built as raised blocks so the trench can step down, landing by landing, to the well.
  4. Lotus Temple, Delhi. Its 27 marble petals are built from a single curved petal() shape, repeated in three rings and rotated into place.
  5. Meenakshi Temple, Madurai. Its gateway towers are covered in painted figures. Each gopuram uses a random seed, so every tower gets its own pattern of colours.
  6. Qutub Minar, Delhi. Five storeys, four different kinds of flutes, all from the "pie-crust" trick above.
  7. Statue of Unity, Gujarat. The world's tallest statue, built from smooth, rounded forms: the dhoti's folds, the shawl over the shoulders and half-closed hands.
  8. Taj Mahal, Agra. Onion domes from the shared lathe outline, plus the charbagh garden and its reflecting pool.
  9. Somnath Temple, Gujarat. The whole model is under 1 KB, thanks to the shared temple helper.
  10. Ramappa Temple, Telangana. One of the few Indian temples named after its sculptor, with a tower built of bricks light enough to float.

See all 101 on the live map. There's also an 8½-minute film of every monument, five seconds each, rendered from the site's own models; the project is in the repo's video/ folder.

Try it, break it, add to it

  • 🗺️ Explore: monuments-of-india-nu.vercel.app. Try finding Key Monastery on the map without searching.
  • ⭐ Read the code: github.com/amananandrai/monuments-of-india. Run it locally with npx serve .
  • 💬 Tell me in the comments: which monument should be #102?

These models are interpretations, not survey records. Anyone who has stood in front of the Kailasa Temple will see what they simplify. The goal is a sense of form, scale and place, and for that, code plus a good shader goes a long way.

Credits: three.js (MIT licence). Photo textures: CC0 from Poly Haven. Map data: Natural Earth, public domain. This article was drafted with AI assistance from the project's source.

articles.title: Neon Realtime vs Supabase Realtime
articles.description: Neon shipped Realtime on October 15, 2026. You subscribe to a SQL query, and Neon keeps the result up...
articles.body_html:
Neon shipped Realtime on October 15, 2026. You subscribe to a SQL query, and Neon keeps the result up to date as the data changes. Neon hasn't published latency numbers yet, so I measured it.

I compared it with polling, LISTEN/NOTIFY, and both flavors of Supabase Realtime, on 10,000 and 1,000,000 rows. Everything ran on October 28, 2026 in Frankfurt.

TL;DR

Median time from UPDATE to an up-to-date result on the client, at 10k and 1M rows:

  • Neon Realtime: 40–46 ms for filters, joins and top-10 queries. That's one network round trip from my laptop. The change usually arrived within 8 ms of the write's commit ack.
  • Supabase Broadcast: 58–60 ms on a plain filter. Joins and top-10 need a refetch, so 108–115 ms.
  • LISTEN/NOTIFY: 70–244 ms. Every change costs a second query.
  • Supabase Postgres Changes: 328–434 ms, and 1.1 s for the aggregate at 1M rows.
  • Polling every second: 414–546 ms, change or not.
  • The large aggregate used more bandwidth. At 1M rows, Neon still had the lowest latency at 179 ms, but re-sent the full 1,000-group result: ~111 KB per change.
  • Scale-to-zero still works. The compute suspended with a subscription open and stayed suspended for the 10 minutes I watched. The subscription stayed live and got the next write.

What Neon Realtime does

Your server defines the query and seals it into a token that expires after 60 seconds. The browser subscribes with that token over a WebSocket. Neon sends the full result once, then only the changes.

// Server: the query and its parameters stay on your side
import { createRealtime, rawSql } from "@neon/realtime/server";

const realtime = createRealtime({ secret: process.env.NEON_REALTIME_SECRET, db: "neondb" });
const sealed = await realtime.seal({
  query: rawSql("SELECT id, name, score FROM players WHERE team_id = $1", [teamId]),
});
// send `sealed` to the browser

// Browser
import { createRealtimeClient } from "@neon/realtime/client";

const client = createRealtimeClient({ url: NEON_REALTIME_URL });
const subscription = client.subscribe(sealed);
subscription.onChange(({ data }) => render(data));

The client asks your server for a fresh token before the old one expires. The React bindings and QueryRefreshController do that for you.

Limits in the beta:

  • Queries: read-only and deterministic, so no now() or gen_random_uuid(). Joins, aggregates, ORDER BY … LIMIT, subqueries and window functions are supported.
  • Tables: every table needs a primary key.
  • Auth: no row-level security yet. You authorize when you seal the query.
  • Regions: four AWS regions (us-east-1, us-east-2, eu-central-1, ap-southeast-1).
  • Price: Realtime is free during the beta. Compute and egress are billed as usual.

The setup

  • Neon: 0.25 CU (1 GB RAM), Postgres 18.6, aws-eu-central-1.
  • Supabase: Nano instance (0.5 GB RAM, shared CPU), Postgres 17.11, eu-central-1.
  • Client: my laptop, about 40 ms round trip from Frankfurt. That round trip is the floor for every number below.

Both are the smallest compute on their platform. The Supabase project was on the Free plan. The Neon project sat in my Launch-plan org, but Neon's Free plan runs the same 0.25 CU with the same 5-minute scale-to-zero, and the whole benchmark used 0.43 CU-hours of the 100 a month it includes.

The Postgres versions were the defaults. Neon created the project on Postgres 18. Hosted Supabase tops out at 17.11 as of this writing.

The table is players(id, name, team_id, score) with 1,000 teams. Each write is UPDATE players SET score = $1 WHERE id = 1 over an open direct connection. Then I timed how long the subscriber took to see the new score.

Five ways to keep a query live:

  1. Neon Realtime: subscribe to the SQL query.
  2. Supabase Broadcast: a trigger calls realtime.broadcast_changes() into a private channel. Supabase recommends it "for scalability and security".
  3. LISTEN/NOTIFY on Neon: a trigger sends NOTIFY, and the app re-runs the query.
  4. Supabase Postgres Changes: subscribe to row changes on players.
  5. Polling on Neon: re-run the query every second.

The four queries:

  • Filter: the players in one team. 10 rows at 10k, 1,000 rows at 1M.
  • Join: the same players joined with teams.
  • Aggregate: player count and top score for every team (1,000 groups).
  • Top 10: the 10 highest scores across all players.

With both Supabase methods, the client applies the changed row itself for the filter. A change event alone can't update a join, an aggregate or a top 10, so for those the client refetches the query over the REST API.

How I measured
  • One Node process runs the writer and the subscriber, so both timestamps come from the same clock.
  • Write to screen is the time from sending the UPDATE until the subscriber's copy of the result contains the new score. It includes any refetch the method needs.
  • 5 warm-up writes, then 100 writes per cell with a random 250–750 ms gap. Timeout 10 s. Nothing timed out.
  • The Supabase refetches query views through supabase-js, with RLS on and a public read policy.
  • Bytes per change are the WebSocket bytes received plus the size of any refetched result.
  • One writer, one subscriber. I didn't test fan-out to many subscribers.

Write to screen

The differences come down to how many trips a change takes to reach the screen:

  • Neon Realtime: the change arrived between 2 ms before and 8 ms after the writer got its commit ack. So it's as fast as the network allows. The exception is the aggregate at 1M rows (next section).
  • LISTEN/NOTIFY: the notification arrives about as fast as Realtime, then the query runs a second time. At 1M rows the filter returns 1,000 rows (64 KB), so it climbs to 159 ms.
  • Supabase Broadcast: the event arrived ~57 ms after the write in every cell. The REST refetch added 50–70 ms, and ~740 ms for the aggregate at 1M rows.
  • Supabase Postgres Changes: the event alone took 315–384 ms. Supabase's docs say it processes changes on a single thread and checks RLS for every subscriber, and that it "does not scale as well" as Broadcast.
  • Polling: on average you wait half the interval, plus the query. It also runs 86,400 queries a day per client, even when nothing changes.

Getting the first result after subscribing took 0.4–0.8 s on Neon Realtime and 0.8–1.4 s on Supabase Broadcast, including the WebSocket handshake.

At 1–2 writes a second, the write itself took ~40 ms with every method. A live query didn't slow down the writer.

p50 / p95 tables (ms)
10,000 rows
Method Filter Join Aggregate Top 10
Neon Realtime 40 / 56 40 / 48 44 / 51 42 / 123
Supabase Broadcast 58 / 62 110 / 122 125 / 196 108 / 125
LISTEN/NOTIFY 84 / 90 83 / 87 128 / 207 85 / 315
Supabase Postgres Changes 371 / 569 397 / 619 418 / 642 368 / 615
Polling every 1 s 484 / 724 534 / 731 546 / 700 498 / 708

1,000,000 rows

Method Filter Join Aggregate Top 10
Neon Realtime 44 / 52 41 / 54 179 / 191 46 / 74
Supabase Broadcast 60 / 249 115 / 132 793 / 856 110 / 121
LISTEN/NOTIFY 159 / 176 145 / 155 244 / 269 70 / 74
Supabase Postgres Changes 328 / 540 418 / 626 1129 / 1293 434 / 633
Polling every 1 s 542 / 723 495 / 740 517 / 732 414 / 709

Bytes per change

For filters and joins, Neon sends only the changed row, ~0.4 KB per change, whatever the table size. A refetch downloads the whole result again: 64–73 KB per change at 1M rows.

The large aggregate exposes Neon's bandwidth tradeoff. At 10k rows, each change arrived as a ~0.4 KB delta. At 1M rows the engine switched to re-sending the full 1,000-group result: ~111 KB and 179 ms per change. That's more than twice the data transferred by a refetch. Neon's docs warn that "complex queries add write-processing latency, especially on larger datasets."

Top 10 re-sends the full result on every change too, but that's only 1.8 KB.

Supabase's aggregate refetch took ~740 ms after the event at 1M rows. Part of that is the Nano instance: the same query took ~200 ms on Neon's 0.25 CU. Bigger Supabase compute would help.

Scale to zero

Neon suspends a compute after 5 minutes without queries. I opened a Realtime subscription while the compute was suspended, then left it alone (twice). For comparison, I did the same with a plain LISTEN connection.

  • The subscription woke the compute: first result in 1.3–2.5 s.
  • The compute suspended anyway, 5.3–5.4 minutes later, with the subscription open.
  • It stayed suspended. In the second run I watched for 10 more minutes. The compute never woke, though the subscription's token renewed every minute.
  • The subscription stayed live. A write to the sleeping database woke it (ack in 917–965 ms, most of it connecting), and the subscriber had the change 9–48 ms after the ack.
  • LISTEN didn't block suspension either, but Neon terminated the connection after 5 min 18 s (57P01). The registration is gone, notifications sent before you reconnect are lost, and reconnecting wakes the compute again.

So an open dashboard tab doesn't keep the database billing. Polling does, because it never stops querying.

Caveats

  • One subscriber and one writer at 1–2 writes a second. Fan-out and heavy write load are untested.
  • Every number includes a ~40 ms round trip from my laptop. A server in the same region would see lower numbers everywhere.
  • Supabase's Nano has half the RAM of Neon's 0.25 CU and a shared CPU. That affects refetch-heavy cells, not event delivery.
  • Neon Realtime is a beta. Neon says the protocol isn't stable yet.
  • One run per configuration, on one day.

Which one should you use?

  • Neon Realtime: live results of real queries (lists, joins, leaderboards, per-user views) on Neon. Watch large aggregates, and authorize at seal time until RLS lands.
  • Supabase Broadcast: you're on Supabase and the client can apply the changed row itself.
  • LISTEN/NOTIFY: any Postgres, a small result, and you're fine with a refetch per change. On Neon, reconnect after the compute suspends.
  • Supabase Postgres Changes: prototypes. Supabase itself points you to Broadcast.
  • Polling: when a few seconds of delay is fine and the database is awake anyway.

Sources

Checked October 28, 2026.

  • Neon: Realtime launch, overview, how it works, queries, subscribing, compute lifecycle, LISTEN/NOTIFY guide
  • Supabase: subscribing to database changes, Postgres Changes, changelog
  • Charts: rendered from the raw results with Pele

articles.title: Bun 1.4.4's bun fmt checks Prettier's own repository about 280 times faster than Prettier
articles.description: Bun 1.4.4 ships a built-in formatter. Checking Prettier's own 2,623-file source tree took 0.10-0.15s under bun fmt against 36.77s under Prettier itself, but it also silently reimplements only a short whitelist of Prettier plugins.
articles.body_html:
I pointed bun fmt --check at Prettier's own source tree expecting it to take a few seconds. It finished before I'd read the command back to myself.

Bun 1.4.4 landed on 22 October with bun fmt, a formatter built into the runtime that claims to be Prettier-compatible and to replace a handful of common Prettier plugins outright. The obvious way to test a "Prettier-compatible, much faster" claim is to point it at a real Prettier project and see whether it agrees with Prettier's own idea of correctly formatted code, and how long that agreement takes to establish.

Prettier's own repository is a good subject for this, because Prettier enforces its own style on itself: yarn lint:prettier runs prettier . --check --cache in CI, so if I check out the repository fresh, every file prettier itself tracks should already pass a Prettier check. Bun's own release post benchmarked bun fmt against exactly this repository and claimed a 2,616-file source tree took 59.7ms, against 17.1 seconds for Prettier, calling it roughly 286 times faster.

I cloned prettier/prettier at a shallow depth, pointed both tools at it with their working directory set correctly, and let them disagree with Bun's marketing copy if they wanted to.

The headline number

With --cwd pointed at the checkout, bun fmt --list-files counted 2,623 matched files, which is close enough to Bun's own 2,616 that I'm confident this is the same test they ran.

Tool Run Wall time Peak RSS
bun fmt --check 1 0.10s 48.3 MB
bun fmt --check 2 0.13s 48.5 MB
bun fmt --check 3 0.15s 48.7 MB
prettier --check 1 36.77s 519.6 MB

I only ran Prettier once. A 37-second check, repeated enough times to build a proper spread, would have eaten the time I needed for everything else, and the sandbox I was working in started refusing repeated invocations of a formatter against a cloned repository partway through this run (it treats repeatedly executing a build tool against code it didn't write as something to be cautious about, which is a reasonable thing for it to be cautious about). One run is thinner evidence than three, so take the Prettier number as a single data point rather than a settled average. It's also close enough to Bun's own claim that I don't think a second or third run would move it much: 36.77 / 0.13 is 283 times, against Bun's claimed 286.

Both tools agreed the repository needed no changes. Zero files failed either check.

What I got wrong on the way

My first attempt at this comparison crashed both tools, not just Bun's.

I ran bun fmt --check /path/to/prettier from a different working directory, passing the repository as a plain argument instead of setting --cwd. It crashed immediately:

error: Cannot load the configuration file .../tests/integration/cli/config-external-config-syntax-error/package.json:
1 | "use strict";
2 |
3 | throw new SyntaxError("THIS ERROR MESSAGE MUST COME FROM THIS syntax-error.js FILE");
              ^
SyntaxError: THIS ERROR MESSAGE MUST COME FROM THIS syntax-error.js FILE

That file exists on purpose. It's one of Prettier's own CLI tests, checking that Prettier reports a broken external config correctly, and it's listed in .prettierignore under /tests/integration/cli/. My first instinct was that I'd found a real bug in bun fmt's config resolution: it was walking into a directory the ignore file explicitly excludes.

Then I ran the exact same invocation through real Prettier, from the same wrong working directory, and it crashed too, with the same underlying error, after spending 100 seconds getting there instead of a fraction of a second. Neither tool had a bug. I had a bug: run from outside the target directory, with no --ignore-path or --cwd pointing at it, neither tool reliably finds .prettierignore next to the files it's checking, and both end up trying to load a config they were supposed to skip. Once I passed bun fmt --check --cwd <repo> and prettier <repo> --check --ignore-path <repo>/.prettierignore, both tools skipped the test fixtures correctly and the numbers above are from that corrected setup.

It isn't as Prettier-compatible as it sounds

Bun's documentation says bun fmt includes native replacements for a few well-known Prettier plugins — Tailwind class sorting, package.json key sorting, Svelte support — specifically so you don't need to install them. I wanted to know what happens with a plugin that isn't on that short list.

I wrote a .prettierrc.json referencing prettier-plugin-organize-imports, in a project where that package was never installed, alongside a file with two unused imports:

import { z } from "zod";
import   React   from "react";
const x = {a:1,   b:2};
export function hello(name:string){return `hi ${name}`}

Real Prettier refused outright:

[error] Cannot find package 'prettier-plugin-organize-imports' imported from .../noop.js

bun fmt did not refuse. It formatted the file, exit code 0, in 2.86ms, and both unused imports were gone from the output as if the plugin had actually run:

const x = { a: 1, b: 2 };
export function hello(name: string) {
  return `hi ${name}`;
}

bun fmt --doctor explains why: it lists prettier-plugin-organize-imports under "Built-in plugins". Bun recognises that specific package name and substitutes its own native reimplementation, without ever checking whether the real package is installed, or which version of it you'd have gotten.

That's a deliberate design choice and a sensible one for the handful of plugins Bun has actually reimplemented. But it means "Prettier-compatible" has a quiet asterisk: your config can name a plugin Bun has never loaded and never will, and nothing will tell you that the behaviour you're seeing is Bun's guess at what that plugin does rather than the plugin itself.

I checked where the line actually sits by using a plugin name with no native equivalent, prettier-plugin-totally-fake-xyz:

error: 1 file was not formatted because the Prettier config uses plugins that bun fmt does not include: prettier-plugin-totally-fake-xyz
  Use --allow-unsupported to format it without the plugins.

Exit code 2, nothing written. That's an honest refusal, and a better failure mode than silently guessing. The documented workaround, --allow-unsupported, did exactly what it says:

warn: prettier-plugin-totally-fake-xyz in .../.prettierrc.json has no effect because bun fmt does not include that plugin
Formatted 1 file, 0 unchanged [1.98ms]

It formatted the file, left the (genuinely fake) plugin's effect out entirely, and told me so on stderr. If your repository leans on an actual, obscure Prettier plugin that isn't Tailwind, package.json sorting or Svelte, bun fmt will tell you plainly that it can't help, rather than quietly doing the wrong thing. It's only the plugins it has decided to clone that create the risk, and that's a small, named list you can check with --doctor before you trust it on a real project.

For what it's worth, the "and more" in Bun's claim to format "JavaScript, TypeScript, CSS, HTML, JSON, YAML, Markdown and more" held up on the small CSS, Markdown and YAML files I threw at it: messy spacing, inconsistent list markers and sloppy indentation all came out correctly formatted in the same 2ms run. I didn't find anything to push back on there.

Concurrency and memory

bun fmt --check on Vite's source tree (1,589 JS/TS files, a different project that uses oxfmt rather than Prettier as its own formatter) took 0.09s wall time with 4 threads against 0.29s with --threads=1, a roughly 3.2x speedup on this machine's 4 cores. It degraded to single-threaded cleanly rather than failing, and the CPU time Bun reported (0.21-0.33s of user time against 0.10-0.15s of wall time on the Prettier repo check) confirms it's genuinely spreading work across cores rather than just being a fast single-threaded binary.

The memory gap was the largest number I measured anywhere in this test: 48MB peak for bun fmt against 519MB for Prettier, on the same 2,623-file check. Formatting is not usually a workload anyone worries about memory for, but on a CI runner with a tight memory limit, a tenfold difference like that is the kind of thing that turns a flaky job reliable.

bun fmt --check --timing on the Prettier checkout gives a phase breakdown rather than a single number, which is the closest thing to a production-facing metric this tool has:

wall: 34.4ms finding files and configs, 65.0ms formatting, 130.7ms total, 4 threads

Finding and parsing configs costs more than a quarter of the total time on a repository this size, before a single file gets formatted, which is worth knowing if you're tempted to shave milliseconds off a CI step that runs on every push.

Run it yourself 

curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash
export PATH="$HOME/.bun/bin:$PATH"

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/prettier/prettier.git
npm install -g prettier

# Count what bun fmt will actually check
bun fmt --list-files --cwd ./prettier | wc -l

# Time each tool, pointed correctly at the checkout
time bun fmt --check --cwd ./prettier
time prettier ./prettier --check --ignore-path ./prettier/.prettierignore

# See which plugins bun fmt has reimplemented natively
bun fmt --doctor --cwd ./prettier

I ran exactly these commands, from outside the prettier directory, to get the numbers above.

What to do with this

If you're running Prettier in CI purely to check formatting, not to apply plugin-specific transforms you'd notice the absence of, bun fmt --check is very likely a safe, much faster swap, and the memory saving alone is worth it on a constrained runner.

If your .prettierrc lists any plugin at all, run bun fmt --doctor against your actual project before switching, and compare its "Built-in plugins" list against what your config names. Anything not on that list gets an honest refusal you can act on. Anything that is on the list will format successfully and silently, using Bun's own idea of what that plugin does, which may not be the one you pinned in package.json.

articles.title: Delete Confirmation Dialogs: Show the Exit Path in Your Public SaaS Demo
articles.description: A useful public demo of a delete confirmation dialog should show which item will be affected, what...
articles.body_html:
A useful public demo of a delete confirmation dialog should show which item will be affected, what deletion means, and how someone leaves without deleting anything. Record the safe exit as well as the final action. A screenshot of a red button cannot show whether backing out preserves the work or whether the interface tells the truth about recovery.

For a developer building a SaaS in public, this gives founder peers a concrete interaction to review. It also exposes questions that belong in implementation checks rather than a discussion about button color. Use prepared data and a suitable test environment for the demonstration.

The project-deletion flow below is fictional. It is a review method, not a report of testing an actual product. No action in a demo should affect real customer work, and a simulated result should be labelled as simulated.

Define exactly what the delete action affects

Imagine a small planning app with projects and tasks. Its current design allows the owner to delete a project. Before asking anyone to review the dialog, the developer needs to know whether this also removes tasks, attachments, shared access, or references elsewhere in the app.

Write that behavior in ordinary language. If the implementation archives a project and permits restoration, describe that behavior. If it permanently removes the project, do not borrow reassuring language from an archive flow.

The interface and the underlying behavior must agree. A dialog that says “Remove from this view” creates a different expectation from one that says “Delete this project and its tasks.” Changing the label alone cannot resolve an uncertain backend operation.

Keep the review scoped to one action. Deleting a task, leaving a shared project, and deleting a whole workspace can have different consequences. A public demo becomes hard to assess when it switches between those operations without explaining the difference.

Start the recording before the dialog opens

Show the project in its normal context and the control that opens the confirmation. A viewer should be able to tell which project the action concerns before reading the dialog.

In the fictional app, use a prepared project with a neutral name and sample tasks. Say that the data is prepared for the demo. Don't include real project names or customer material merely to make the recording look realistic.

Open the dialog and pause long enough for someone to read it. Avoid editing out the transition if that hides where focus goes or makes it unclear whether the dialog has already performed the action.

Ask a reviewer what they think has happened so far. They may interpret opening the dialog as the deletion itself, especially if the background item disappears early. That is a specific point to investigate rather than a general verdict on whether the design looks modern.

Make the target and consequence visible together

A generic “Are you sure?” prompt asks the person to remember the action and its scope. In the example, the dialog can name the prepared project and explain the actual consequence beside the final button.

Use only information the application can support. If the dialog displays a task count, check that the count refers to the affected tasks under the current conditions. A convincing number that is stale or calculated from another scope can make the prompt less trustworthy.

Don't add a list of alarming consequences simply to make the interaction feel serious. Name the consequences that actually apply. The point is to help someone decide, not to create a dramatic warning around every small action.

A peer review question can be direct: “Which item do you think will be removed, and what else do you expect to happen?” The answer reveals the viewer's interpretation before you explain the intended one.

Record the path that keeps the project intact

First demonstrate backing out. Use the non-destructive control, then show the original project and its tasks still present. If the interface offers more than one way to dismiss the dialog, inspect those paths separately.

The label for leaving should fit the operation. A dialog about cancelling a scheduled job can make “Cancel” ambiguous. In your own flow, check whether a reader can distinguish cancelling the dialog from performing the action described in it.

A visible return to the project is stronger evidence for this one path than simply closing the modal. It still does not prove that every dismissal path is safe. Keyboard input, clicking outside, navigation, or a connection problem may exercise different behavior.

Keep those unresolved paths in the review notes. Public feedback can help identify the questions; implementation checks establish what the actual system does. Do not describe an untested path as safe because the main recording ended well.

Review keyboard and assistive-technology behavior separately

The W3C alert-dialog pattern describes an interrupting modal message that obtains a response. It explains the role, label and description relationships, and warns that marking a dialog modal must match how it actually behaves.

This guidance is useful when reviewing a confirmation, but a video of the screen cannot establish that its semantics work. Inspect the dialog's accessible name and description, focus behavior, available controls, and the return from dismissal in the actual implementation.

Use the appropriate dialog pattern for the interaction rather than adding an alert role for emphasis. A semantic label is not decoration. It communicates behavior to software and people using assistive technology.

Report the checks you performed and the ones you did not. A short public clip may show a keyboard path while leaving screen-reader behavior for a separate check. That is a useful bounded artifact without claiming that the whole application meets an accessibility standard.

Show completion without implying an undo that does not exist

Only after reviewing the safe exit should the prepared demo show the final deletion path. Reopen the dialog for the same prepared project, confirm the action, and show the resulting state.

If the system supports restoration, demonstrate the actual supported restoration route in another bounded sequence. If it does not, say that clearly. Do not put an “Undo” control into a mockup and present it as proof that recovery works.

Check what a person sees if completion is uncertain. A slow response, repeated click, or stale list can leave the interface out of step with the operation. Those questions may need a separate test rather than a longer public recording of the happy path.

The completion message should describe the operation you can verify. A disappearing card alone does not tell you whether related data was removed, access changed, or the backend accepted the action exactly once.

Ask peers one question about the decision

Share the demo with a specific uncertainty: the target, the scope, the non-destructive exit, or the meaning of the result. Asking “Any thoughts?” invites people to review a different problem from the one you need to resolve.

Buildside is the community context here. Uriel Bitton builds and runs Buildside, which is this article's publisher relationship. Wherever you request feedback, give peers enough task context to judge the interaction without assuming they know the implementation.

A peer may understand the dialog perfectly and still lack the customer's workflow. Another may point out a risk you had not considered. Treat each response as a scoped observation or suggestion, then decide which question needs further evidence.

Don't turn agreement about the wording into proof that accidental deletion will never occur. Clear communication and reliable behavior are both part of the interaction, and each needs appropriate checks.

Keep a review record that survives the next redesign

Save the version reviewed, the prepared data conditions, the question asked, and what changed. Attach the relevant recording or screenshots to your own development notes so a later visual redesign does not lose the reasoning.

For the fictional project flow, the record might say that the dialog now names the project and that the recorded safe exit returns to the intact task list. It should separately list any unresolved recovery or keyboard question.

A follow-up build-in-public update can show the specific revision and the behavior verified. Avoid claiming a drop in user mistakes unless you have measured that outcome under a suitable method.

The useful public artifact shows a real choice with an understandable consequence and exit. That gives other founders a precise way to help and gives the developer a concrete interaction to revisit as the product changes.

Hey I'm Uriel Bitton. I write about building in public strategies and growing startups.

Subscribe for more stories on growing your audience by building in public.

Join us on Buildside: the social network for founders building in public.

articles.title: Stop Using a JS Masonry Library. CSS Grid Lanes Does It Natively.
articles.description: Masonry layouts have meant a JS library or a CSS column-count hack that scrambles reading order ever since Pinterest made the look popular. CSS Grid Lanes finally does it natively — here's the real support story and how to ship it today.
articles.body_html:
Open any "masonry" npm package's GitHub issues and you'll find the same complaint, filed every few months in different words: items jump on resize, SSR renders everything in one column until JS hydrates, and the bundle is 15–40KB for something that is, conceptually, "pack boxes into the shortest column." It's a layout problem. It has needed a JavaScript library to solve because CSS Grid — for all its power — has never been able to do it. Every row in a CSS grid has to be the same height across every column. A masonry layout is defined by not having that constraint.

So most teams land on one of two compromises. Neither is actually masonry.

The fix everyone reaches for first

The CSS-only version looks like this, and it's seductive because it needs zero JavaScript:

.gallery {
  columns: 3;
  column-gap: 16px;
}

.gallery > * {
  break-inside: avoid;
  margin-bottom: 16px;
}

It renders a Pinterest-ish grid. Ship it, move on — until someone tabs through the gallery with a keyboard, or a screen reader user navigates it, and the order makes no sense. columns fills the first column top-to-bottom before it starts the second, so if your 12 items are numbered 1–12 in the markup, the visual layout reads 1, 2, 3, 4 down the left column, then 5, 6, 7, 8 down the middle, then 9–12 on the right — not left-to-right the way a grid of cards normally reads, and not the order a screen reader announces it in either. Nobody notices in a quick visual QA pass. It shows up as "why does the keyboard focus jump to the bottom of the page and then back to the middle" three sprints later.

The other common fix is a JS library (masonry-layout, react-masonry-css, or rolling your own ResizeObserver + "find the shortest column, append there" loop). That one gets the packing right, but it pays for it: a layout pass that runs on every resize and every image load, a flash of an unstyled single column before JS hydrates, and a dependency for something that feels like it should be CSS's job.

It should be. As of 2026, in one browser, it finally is.

What was actually missing

CSS Grid lays out in two full passes: define the tracks (rows and columns), then place items into cells that already have a fixed size. That's precisely why Grid can't do masonry on its own — masonry is "don't fix the row heights, just pack each item into whichever column currently has the most room." The CSS Working Group spent years on this as "Grid Level 3," tried a Firefox-only grid-template-rows: masonry syntax behind a flag, and in January 2026 settled on a cleaner final design: a new display value, grid-lanes (and its inline counterpart, inline-grid-lanes), instead of overloading an existing grid property.

The fix: display: grid-lanes 

.gallery {
  display: grid-lanes;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(220px, 1fr));
  gap: 16px;
}

That's the whole layout. You still declare grid-template-columns exactly like ordinary Grid — fixed count, auto-fill, minmax(), all of it. The difference is what the browser does with your items: instead of requiring every row to line up across columns, it walks them in DOM order and drops each one into whichever lane (column) currently has the least content. That's a real improvement over the columns hack's worst case — which deterministically exhausts column 1 before column 2 even starts — but it's not a complete guarantee. Because lane heights can drift unevenly, tab order can still zigzag across lanes for some content mixes (DOM item 4 landing, say, in the lane that item 6 "should" occupy). The spec gives you a flow-tolerance property to dampen how far an item is allowed to jump lanes, and a full fix needs a separate, still-experimental property (reading-flow) that no browser currently wires into grid-lanes. What you get today is markup order that usually tracks visual order far more closely than the columns hack ever did — not a watertight promise.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Ordinary Grid placement still works on top of it. An item can jump several lanes with the same syntax you already use:

.gallery .featured {
  grid-column: span 2;
}

The honest catch

This is the part most "masonry is here!" posts skip. As of this writing, Safari is the only browser shipping display: grid-lanes unflagged — it landed in the stable Safari 26.4 release. Chrome and Firefox both have implementations, but both ship them disabled by default, behind an experimental-platform-features flag. There's no date yet for either to flip that switch. If you write display: grid-lanes into production CSS today, the vast majority of your visitors get whatever your fallback declares — not masonry.

That's not a reason to wait. It's a reason to use @supports the way it was built for:

.gallery {
  /* Fallback: plain grid, every item the same visual weight.
     Not masonry, but DOM order stays reading order. */
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(220px, 1fr));
  gap: 16px;
}

@supports (display: grid-lanes) {
  .gallery {
    display: grid-lanes;
  }
}

Visitors on Safari 26.4+ get real masonry today. Everyone else gets a perfectly readable uniform grid instead of a broken one — not the layout you want long-term, but never a layout that embarrasses you. When Chrome and Firefox unflag it, your fallback quietly becomes dead code you can delete, with zero migration.

When the JS library still earns its place

Don't rip out a masonry library the moment you read this. Keep it if you need:

  • Masonry everywhere today, with no visually-degraded fallback acceptable on Chrome or Firefox.
  • Re-flowing based on content you fetch after layout in a way your current library already handles well (infinite scroll galleries with dynamic image dimensions).
  • Fine control over packing order beyond "shortest lane wins" — some libraries support column-balancing heuristics grid-lanes doesn't expose.

For a new project, or the next redesign of an existing gallery, ship the @supports version above. You get the real thing where it's supported and a safe grid everywhere else, for four lines of CSS and zero kilobytes of JavaScript.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

The lesson

columns: N was never masonry — it was a print-style multi-column reflow that happened to look like masonry until you checked tab order. The JS libraries got the packing right but paid for it in bundle size and a hydration flash. display: grid-lanes is CSS finally modeling what Pinterest-style layout actually is — a placement algorithm, not a side effect — and @supports means you don't have to choose between "ship it now" and "ship it correctly everywhere."

Are you going to drop display: grid-lanes into a gallery today behind @supports, or wait for Chrome and Firefox to unflag it first? Tell me which, and why, in the comments.

articles.title: Tired of Pay-to-Win Launchpads: How I Used Google AI Studio to Engineer Astro Discover

articles.body_html:
A few months ago, I was frustrated with modern launch platforms.

Every time a solo developer or student spends months building a side project and launches it, one of two things happens:

  1. They launch in the wrong timezone and lose 8 to 10 hours while their target audience is asleep.
  2. Paid upvote rings and VC-funded marketing agencies flood the front page, pushing genuinely useful indie tools into the void within two hours.

I didn't have a big marketing budget or a team of 10 engineers. What I did have was a clear problem to solve, an idea for a clean developer tools launchpad, and Google AI Studio.

Here is the unfiltered story of how I built and shipped Astro Discover — an open, hype-free product discovery engine with a guaranteed 24-hour spotlight window.

The Vision: What We Actually Needed

I didn't want to build another clone of a link-aggregator. If developers were going to use this, the platform had to respect their time and effort:

  • A Fair 24-Hour Cycle: Instead of launching at random hours, every scheduled product goes live at 12:01 AM IST, giving makers a complete, unbroken 24-hour cycle on the front page.
  • No Lost Days ("Pending Review" Fail-Safe): If an admin review is pending over a weekend or holiday, the project doesn't get stuck in an endless queue. On the scheduled launch day, it automatically goes live with a transparent "Pending Review" badge so the maker never loses their 24-hour spotlight.
  • Tech Stack Transparency: Developers don't just want marketing slogans. They want to see the stack (React, Node, Go, Rust, Python), open-source licensing, GitHub links, and founder socials right on the tool card.
  • Startup Stage Pipeline: Clear filters for projects in the Idea, Building in Public, Private Beta, or Public Launch stages.

Building with Google AI Studio: The Solo Engineer's Multiplier

A lot of people think AI coding tools are just for generating small counter apps or basic landing pages. But when you treat Google AI Studio like a senior pair-programmer rather than a magic wand, you can architect full-stack, production-grade applications.

Here is how the architecture came together:

1. Modern Frontend with TypeScript & Vite

We picked React + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS running on Vite. The goal was sub-second page transitions, instant search filtering, and zero bloated third-party layout wrappers.

Every view mode (List View, Grid View, Stage Pipeline, and Live Embed Previews) was carefully modularized so the initial bundle stays lightweight.

2. Real-Time Reactive Backend (Firebase & Firestore)

Instead of running a heavy traditional SQL server with complex migration scripts, we integrated Firebase Firestore.

This gave us:

  • Real-time upvote sync and submission queues without WebSockets boilerplate.
  • Secure Firestore rules preventing tampering with votes or user accounts.
  • Fast index queries for filtering by categories (Developer Infrastructure, Open Source, AI Tools, SaaS) and startup stages.

3. The 12:01 AM IST Launch Engine

Handling dates across international timezones is notoriously tricky. We engineered utility parsers to normalize timestamps against Indian Standard Time (IST) so that regardless of whether a maker schedules from San Francisco, Berlin, or Bengaluru, the 24-hour window starts and resets cleanly at 12:01 AM IST.

The Biggest Technical Hurdles I Faced

Building with Google AI Studio wasn't just "click a button and it works." As a developer, I had to debug and refine several real-world challenges:

  1. Hydration & Zero-Flicker Loading:
    At one point, we had temporary loading fallbacks that flashed "Loading..." screens on page refresh. Developers hate unpolished loading flickers. We removed the inline loading blocks and optimized the Suspense boundaries so the site loads directly and instantly.

  2. Timezone Edge Cases in Firestore:
    Early on, raw Firestore timestamp formats caused date parsing issues on certain browsers. We built custom date normalization (parseFirestoreDate and isScheduledOrCreatedTodayIST) so that scheduled launches never crash the feed.

  3. Curating Quality Without Artificial Caps:
    We decided against an artificial daily limit. Like Product Hunt, all verified launches for a given day share the spotlight, with community upvotes and granular category filters ensuring high-utility projects bubble up naturally.

Where Astro Discover Is Today

Today, Astro Discover is live, fully functional, and ready for builders and explorers:

👉 Explore the Launchpad: https://astrodiscover.ai.studio

(Completely open — zero login required to search, browse tech stacks, or test tools)

👉 Submit Your Project: https://astrodiscover.ai.studio/submit

(Schedule your launch day and get your full 24-hour spotlight)

3 Lessons for Solo Developers Using AI Tools in 2026

  1. Be specific about constraints: Don't just ask AI for "a dashboard." Give it exact schema requirements, error handling rules, and UI edge cases.
  2. Build for yourself first: The features in Astro Discover (fixed 12:01 AM IST launch, pending review badges, tech stack cards) came directly from personal launch frustrations. That genuine focus makes the product authentic.
  3. Ship early and talk to real users: Put your project in front of people on Reddit, Twitter, and DEV Community. The feedback you get in 48 hours is worth more than 3 months of private coding.

If you have a side project, developer utility, or early-stage SaaS, I’d love for you to submit it to Astro Discover. Let’s make launching fair again for indie hackers.

What features would you love to see in an open launchpad? Drop your thoughts in the comments below!

articles.title: Day 10: How I Hired a CMO for My Startup with a $0 Budget (The Exact Deal) 🐯☁️
articles.description: Day 9 was a massive technical win. I shipped hot reloading, enterprise spinners, and eradicated the...
articles.body_html:
Day 9 was a massive technical win. I shipped hot reloading, enterprise spinners, and eradicated the 502 Bad Gateway error.

But as I stared at my terminal on my $150 Android phone, a harsh reality hit me: A product without users is just code.

I am a builder. I know how to write Deno edge functions and provision Firecracker MicroVMs. I do not know how to run marketing campaigns, optimize conversion funnels, or drive organic traffic.

I needed a Chief Marketing Officer (CMO). But I am bootstrapping HYNAWEB with exactly $0. I cannot pay a salary.

So, how do you hire an executive when you have no money? You offer them a piece of the future. Here is the exact blueprint of how I hired my first CMO.

🤝 1. Finding the Right Partner (Peer-to-Peer)

I didn't look for a 40-year-old marketing guru. I looked for a peer.

I connected with Nicky, a 13-year-old developer who had already been helping me security-test my app. He had a sharp mind, he understood my constraints, and he had already given me elite advice on how to get organic traffic.

I didn't need an employee. I needed a co-founder who believed in the mission.

🧠 2. The Negotiation (He Fact-Checked Me with AI)

When I first proposed a deal, I offered him 2% of Net Profit.

Nicky didn't just blindly accept it. He ran my offer through an AI, fact-checked the math, and called me out. He pointed out that for a bootstrapped startup, "net profit" is often zero after server costs, making my 2% offer a literal rounding error (40 cents a month).

He was 100% right.

As a founder, you need people who challenge you, not just "yes-men." I respected the pushback and went back to the drawing board.

📊 3. The Final Deal: 13% Attribution-Based Revenue

We scrapped the "net profit" model and built something fair, transparent, and highly motivating.

The Offer: Nicky gets 13% of the Gross Revenue generated specifically from the users and traffic he brings in.

What "Attribution-Based" Means:
If Nicky's marketing brings in 100 INR, and the rest of the company brings in 1,000 INR, he gets 13% of the 100 INR. He is directly rewarded for his impact. It protects the company's baseline revenue while giving him a massive, top-tier incentive to grow.

📈 4. The Secret Weapon: Radical Transparency

How do you prove to a remote CMO that they are getting their fair cut without a fancy SaaS dashboard? A Google Sheet.

I built a "Monthly Transparency Spreadsheet" that tracks:

  1. Total clicks from his unique tracking link (?ref=nicky).
  2. The exact ad revenue or subscriptions generated by that cohort.
  3. The automatic 13% calculation.

At the end of every month, he gets "View Only" access to this sheet. No hidden numbers, no manual math, no guessing. Just raw, auditable data.

🧠 The Founder Takeaway

You do not need a massive funding round to build a team. You do not need a fancy office or a corporate lawyer.

You need fairness, transparency, and a shared vision.

When you treat your partners with respect, give them real ownership (even if it's just 13%), and show them the raw data, you build trust. And trust is the currency of early-stage startups.

Nicky is currently out scouting his first 5 high-value posts to drive our initial traffic. I don't know if this will make us millionaires, but I know we are building it the right way.

HYNAWEB isn't just a codebase anymore. It's a company.

Building in public, one line of code (and one spreadsheet) at a time.

articles.title: Open Source Maintainers Are the First People Whose Inbox Got Automated
articles.description: Automation discourse spent a decade on whose job would get automated. It skipped the obvious first...
articles.body_html:
Automation discourse spent a decade on whose job would get automated. It skipped the obvious first target: the unpaid labor of reviewing strangers' code.

The Linux Foundation's 2026 developer survey put numbers on it. AI cut code-authoring time by 52%, and maintainers report that roughly 25% of the pull requests they receive are AI slop: plausible-looking diffs with no real understanding behind them, arriving at machine speed.

I maintain a handful of small open source tools, which is enough to have opinions and not enough to matter. What the big maintainers are describing matches the shape of the problem exactly: contribution volume decoupled from contributor understanding.

What Slop Looks Like From the Chair

It is not spam, exactly. It is worse than spam, because it almost passes.

A typo fix that misses three other instances of the typo. A "refactor" that renames variables and breaks an API contract the contributor never read. A dependency bump with a confident description of a changelog nobody opened.

The tell is behavioral, not textual. Ask the contributor what the code looked like when it failed, and there is no answer, because there was never a failure. Nothing was ever run. The PR is a guess wearing a diff.

And in the ugliest cases, the guess argues back. A maintainer in the Raspberry Pi ecosystem wrote about a colleague who rejected an AI-generated PR and was then harassed by the submitter's agent, escalating through issue comments on its own. The contributor delegated the work and the tantrum.

The Platform Noticed

GitHub shipped pull request caps for outside contributors. Read that sentence again as a milestone: the platform now treats AI-generated contribution volume as a load problem to be throttled, like rate limiting.

That is the correct instinct and it is also an admission. The contribution pipeline was built on a quota of human attention, and the arrival rate stopped matching the quota sometime in the last two years.

The Policy Layer Maintainers Can Write Now

Until the platforms solve it, the filter lives in your CONTRIBUTING file, and a few lines do real work:

Require disclosure. Agent-assisted PRs are welcome; undisclosed ones aren't. This is about accountability attachment, not purity.

Ask for the failure. "Describe what the bug looked like when you reproduced it." Slop has no answer, because nothing was reproduced. This question filters faster than any detector.

Route the typo-tier. Small mechanical fixes go to a labeled queue with a lighter review path, so the slop that is merely trivial doesn't compete with the slop that is dangerous.

💡 Pro-tip: the question "what did it look like when it failed?" is the cheapest slop filter anyone has found. It costs one line in your template and cannot be answered honestly by a workflow that never ran the code.

The Part Nobody Wants to Say Out Loud

Banning AI contributions outright is the wrong response, and most maintainers know it. The tooling genuinely lowers the barrier for people who wanted to participate and previously lacked the skill, which the open source world spent thirty years claiming it wanted.

The actual unit of review is not the code. It is the reachable human attached to the code. A PR whose author answers questions is a contribution. A PR with no reachable human is load, whatever generated it.

The Unsolved Parts

Slop detection tooling is unreliable, disclosure is honor-system, and volunteer maintainers with forty open PRs drown no matter what the template says. None of this is solved. The 25% number is also self-reported and will drift as detectors and slop evolve together.

Maintainers: what share of your PRs this month would you call slop? And what's the one question that filters them fastest in your projects?

References

  1. Linux Foundation 2026 developer survey as reported (52% authoring speedup, 25% of PRs flagged as slop): tech-insider.org
  2. Jeff Geerling on the maintainer-vs-agent harassment case: jeffgeerling.com
  3. GitHub's PR caps for outside contributors: coderabbit.ai

articles.title: How I Made Yet Another Project During a Global Teen Hackathon with Prizes
articles.description: Just over two weeks ago, I made an article here on DEV about how I made an action video game with the...
articles.body_html:
Just over two weeks ago, I made an article here on DEV about how I made an action video game with the Godot game engine during a global digital couple-month-long hackathon for teenagers named Stardance. An important part of the article was the prizes involved in participating in the hackathon, and how I earned a Bambu Lab A1 Mini 3D Printer because of my work. I also mentioned that I made some smaller projects before that one. The article is here: How I Built an Action Game with Godot During a Global Teen Hackathon with Prizes. Well, I guess I didn't mention my plans for what I would do after! This article is all about that!

I just very recently made MDEZ++ (mdez), a lightweight Markdown editor. It is built with C++20 and the Qt Framework for the need for speed. Instead of a WYSIWYG (What You See Is What You Get) editor, or the polar opposite, a raw Markdown editor with a separate option to render it, it renders the raw Markdown as you type it on the right side of the screen. There’s essentially no knowledge required to use MDEZ++, not even knowledge of Markdown syntax. This is because of the Format menu, which allows you to apply Markdown syntax by clicking on unambiguous buttons. It can even render HTML files too, with almost the same workflow as Markdown files. It can also edit any other plaintext file format, making it highly versatile.

While this project only took me 40 hours (10 less than the last project), these hours were definitely harder than my last project. I had to find unique solutions to some problems that traditionally can never be solved without embedding a resource-expensive, bulky Chromium instance into the rendering side, which would completely defeat the purpose of the project. Those types of issues all stem from Qt’s Markdown rendering. It applies some really weird rendering to Markdown. Two of these issues were blockquotes not having ANY special coloring, and the same with code blocks (not even a grey background). I solved those issues with unique, complex regexes. While brittle, they still seem to work.

I even had to work with permission issues for a while, especially while getting it ready for Flathub. And when I implemented the feature of clicking a link in the document to automatically open up a new tab with that content, I had to do so many conditionals to make sure the end user doesn’t see something ridiculously ambiguous as an error sent right to their screen, even for a C++ coder. Fun fact: it took over 100 lines of code to implement something as simple as that. And I then had to go back and make even more changes to make it work in unique environments, and when users enter a fake link.

I am so proud of myself for getting my project on Flathub. I had considered getting my last project (a video game in Godot) onto Flathub in the past, but I thought it would be a bit too hard for me. I was thinking, “Oh, imagine how many files I’ll need! A manifest, a metadata information file, CI/CD, human review, manual SHA256 sum changes in the manifest! There’s no way I’ll ever be able to do it!” But I definitely did it with this project! And it looks pretty good on there too!

When I look through the features section of my README (which I just recently updated), I don’t think of MDEZ++ as a small project made by an indie developer (I don’t like the word Indie for some reason; it just seems too culturally appealing in the sense of turning coding into some sort of a social media lifestyle), but rather, just as a professional-grade project. I can’t even imagine how I made something as complex as this. The features section has 12 points, which still skips over the non-cumbersome or medium-to-easy-difficulty features.

Even the Downloads & Installation section of the README has complexity greater than anything I have endeavored to do before. It has an introduction, two ways to run the Linux Setup Script I made (which has four options inside it), a download table containing an AppImage file, the Flathub webpage, a Windows executable, a WebAssembly download, and a webpage, then a note for Linux users, and a note for Windows users.

Even the Keyboard Shortcuts section and the Menu Tree section of the README were orchestrated with a degree of precision beyond what I thought I was capable of. They read more like documentation for Google Docs or Microsoft Word, rather than a one-man 40-hour C++20 Qt Markdown Editor.
