    area = lambda i: abs((p[prev[i]][0] - p[i][0]) * (p[nxt[i]][1] - p[i][1])
                       - (p[nxt[i]][0] - p[i][0]) * (p[prev[i]][1] - p[i][1])) / 2
    alive = [True] * n; cur = [area(i) for i in range(n)]
    h = [(cur[i], i) for i in range(n)]; heapq.heapify(h)
    order = np.zeros(n, int); r = 0; last = 0.0
    while h and r < n - 3:
        a, i = heapq.heappop(h)
        if not alive[i] or a != cur[i]: continue        # stale heap entry
        last = max(last, a)        # a point can't be worth less than the one removed before it
        alive[i] = False; order[i] = r; r += 1
        pi, ni = prev[i], nxt[i]; nxt[pi] = ni; prev[ni] = pi
        for j in (pi, ni):
            cur[j] = max(area(j), last); heapq.heappush(h, (cur[j], j))
    ...

The last = max(...) line is a common fix for Visvalingam–Whyatt. Without it, removing a point can make a neighbour's triangle smaller than the one just removed, and the ranking stops matching what you see.

The build keeps the 300 highest-ranked points per picture, in order round the outline, and writes them to a JSON file with each point's rank. The inner lines go in the same file as an SVG path.

Step 4: pick the dots in the browser

At run time, picking 50 dots could be as simple as "the 50 highest-ranked points". That nearly works. The problem is detail: a claw or a row of spines has lots of sharp corners, so it ranks highly and soaks up the dots. Ten dots on one claw and a straight run of back with none.

So the picker takes points in rank order but skips any point too close to one it already has. It starts with a minimum gap of the outline's length ÷ (n × 1.6), and relaxes the gap by 15% until n points fit:

export function pick(pts, n) {          // pts: [x, y, rank]
  const N = pts.length; if (n >= N) return pts.map((_, i) => i);
  let L = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) { const a = pts[i], b = pts[(i + 1) % N]; L += Math.hypot(b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1]); }
  const order = pts.map((_, i) => i).sort((a, b) => pts[a][2] - pts[b][2]);
  let dmin = L / (n * 1.6);
  for (;;) {
    const got = [];
    for (const i of order) {
      const p = pts[i];
      if (got.every(j => Math.hypot(pts[j][0] - p[0], pts[j][1] - p[1]) >= dmin)) got.push(i);
      if (got.length === n) return got.sort((a, b) => a - b);   // back in outline order
    }
    dmin *= 0.85;
  }
}

Sorting the result by index puts the dots back in order round the outline, so dot 1 to dot n traces the shape.

Step 5: place the numbers

This took the most work, and it's the part people notice. Each number needs a spot that's:

  • next to its own dot, on the outside of the shape where possible,
  • not on top of another number or another dot,
  • not across a line the child will draw between two dots,
  • not on the drawing's inner lines,
  • and clearly nearer its own dot than any other.

The placer tries 12 angles around the outward direction at 3 distances, and scores each spot. Lower is better:

Problem Cost
Overlaps a number already placed 1,000
Touches another dot 500
Closer to another dot than to its own 200
Crosses a line between two dots 80
Nearly as close to another dot (within 1.35×) 60
On one of the drawing's inner lines 30
Turned away from straight out, or pushed further out a little, growing with the angle and distance

Crowded dots are placed first, while there's still room around them. The 60-point rule is the one I added after watching the output: a number can be technically closest to its own dot and still look like it belongs to the next one. To check it was worth having, I ran today's code with and without that rule at 50 dots across all 17 pictures. Without it, 24 of 850 numbers are unclear. With it, 2.

Step 6: test every combination

There are 17 pictures, 5 counts and 6 ways of counting, and phones show the numbers up to 2× bigger than print. That's too many combinations to check by eye, so the tests check all of them:

test('the numbers never sit on another number or another dot, printed or at the phone sizes', () => {
  for (const k of KEYS) for (const n of DOTS) for (const f of (n <= 30 ? [1, 2] : n <= 50 ? [1, 1.3] : [1])) {
    const Lo = layout(A[k], '1', n, Math.min(190 / A[k].w, 230 / A[k].h) / f);
    // ...every pair of number boxes must not overlap, and no number box may cover another dot
  }
});

Another test checks that every picture at every count has the right number of dots, in outline order, and that no two dots are closer than 2.5 dot radii. One Christmas picture failed that at first: the first candy cane was so tall and thin that 100 dots crowded together on it. I redrew it, and it passed.

What I'd do differently

  • Start from silhouettes, not detailed art. I first tried feeding in the site's detailed coloring-page art. The cute Spinosaurus's outline leaked into its body, and the baby dinosaur lost its egg. Clean, simple line drawings work far better.
  • Write the "can a child read this?" test first. Overlap tests pass long before the output is good enough for a child to use. The "which dot does this number belong to?" check is the one that matters most.
  • Keep the slow work at build time. Tracing and ranking run once per drawing in Python. The browser only sorts 300 points and scores a few thousand candidate spots, so changing the count needs no server at all.

You can try it at Toggle9's dot to dot printables. It prints free with no sign-up, with an answer page if you want one.

Have you built anything that puts labels on a drawing or map? I'd like to hear what scoring you ended up with. Label placement turned out to be the most interesting part of this.

articles.title: Stackroots refuses the install that legacy-peer-deps would hide
articles.description: A check that names a version that fits, or tells you not to install. Hiding the peer error does not remove it.
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

What I Built

Stackroots checks a package against the project before anyone installs it. It looks at peers, deprecations, major jumps, and the Node range. If a published release fits, it prints that install command. If none fits, it says do not install.

The ghost is the conflict that is still in the project after you hide it. Antonello Zanini walks through the usual fixes in How To Fix the npm "Conflicting Peer Dependency" Error. One of them is npm install --legacy-peer-deps. That flag tells npm to skip the peer check and install the newest release anyway. The error disappears. The packages are still incompatible.

Nithin D J built guard-install for a different blind spot: supply-chain risk before install. Mohd. Ibrahim Iqbal built Exorcist for the packages already in a package.json: deprecated, duplicated, stale. Stackroots is the moment before the next install. The package is not in the tree yet. The question is whether it belongs there.

Demo

Open stackroots-three.vercel.app. The sample project field-notes is already loaded. It uses React 19.3.0 and Node >=18 <20.

  1. Type recompose and press Check.
  2. Read the result. No published release of recompose accepts this project. Do not install it. npm install --legacy-peer-deps would only hide this conflict.

The same check from a project folder, on Node 22.18 or newer:

npx @fab-c14/stackroots@0.1.2 check recompose

Exit code 1 means stop. A fix line, when one exists, is the exact npm install name@version. recompose has no fix line on this project, because no published release fits.

Gemma 4 writes a note only after a finding, or when you press Ask Gemma 4. The check does not need a key. The note does. Set GEMINI_API_KEY for that part.

Code

fab-c14 / stackroots

Stackroots

Check a package before it joins a project.

Author: fab-c14

Live site: stackroots-three.vercel.app

Package: @fab-c14/stackroots

Stackroots reads the nearest package.json and lockfile and says whether a package you are about to install fits the roots already there. It prints the finding and, when one exists, the npm install line to use. The check is free.

Give this file to a person or to an agent. The procedure under Instructions for an agent is enough to run the check without the rest of the repository. The same procedure is the project skill at .cursor/skills/stackroots/SKILL.md.

How to run

Node 22.18 or newer.

From the project you want to check:

npx @fab-c14/stackroots report
npx @fab-c14/stackroots check zod
npx @fab-c14/stackroots check zod recompose
npx @fab-c14/stackroots check recompose@0.30.0

npx installs the package from the public npm registry. The command walks up from the current folder until it finds a manifest. It reads package.json…

View on GitHub

Repository: github.com/fab-c14/stackroots

Package: npmjs.com/package/@fab-c14/stackroots

How I Built It

The verdict is ordinary code. It reads package.json and the lockfile, then the public npm record for the package. A peer range this project does not satisfy is an error. A missing required peer is a warning. A new major of a package already installed is an error. Node ranges are compared only when engines.node is set. Names passed together count as installed together. A release that drops a required peer is not treated as a fix.

If the release you asked for has errors, Stackroots looks for the newest non-deprecated stable release that has no errors and still declares the same required peers and the same engines.node. That becomes npm install name@version. If nothing qualifies, there is no install command, and the do line says not to install.

Gemma 4 (gemma-4-31b-it) is the open-weight model on the website. It does not run in the command, and it does not run when the page loads. It receives the project name, the Node range, the root names and versions, and the finding. The raw package.json stays in the browser. The call goes to the Gemini API with storage off. I did not run the model on the laptop. If Gemma is down, the do line is still there.

flowchart TD
  A[package.json and lockfile] --> B[Stackroots check]
  B --> C{Does a published release fit?}
  C -->|yes| D["fix line: npm install name@version"]
  C -->|no| E[do line: do not install]
  B --> F[Gemma 4, only if you ask]

How an agent uses it

The same steps are in the README, under Instructions for an agent. An agent runs them before it adds a dependency.

  1. npx @fab-c14/stackroots report to read the tree.
  2. npx @fab-c14/stackroots check <package> for each package it means to install. A version looks like name@version.
  3. Exit 0 and no error line: it may install the name it checked.
  4. A fix line is the command to run. It does not install the version that was rejected.
  5. A do line that says not to install means stop.
  6. It does not add --legacy-peer-deps. It does not invent a version the command did not print. It does not call Gemma from the command.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A closed chat is happy to say "use legacy-peer-deps" and move on. That installs the package and leaves the conflict. Stackroots will not print that flag as a fix.

Gemma 4 can explain a finding. It cannot choose the version. An agent can follow the exit code with no model at all. The package file does not have to leave the machine for the check. Only a short brief of public facts goes out, and only when someone asks for the note.

Exorcist keeps a health scan in the browser so a package.json is not uploaded for scoring. Stackroots keeps the raw file in the browser for a different job: a yes or no on the package you are about to add. Read Exorcist. Read the peer-dependency guide. Read guard-install.

The Spirit of It

I loaded a React 19 project and typed recompose. People still reach for it. Every published release wants an older React. The page did not offer a clever version. It said do not install it, and it said the legacy flag would only hide the conflict.

That is the ghost. It is a library that still installs if you tell npm to look away.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma. Gemma 4 (gemma-4-31b-it) writes the note and answers the chat on the website, only after a finding or a button press. The check does not call it.

articles.description: How I Cut 60% of the Bundle and 76% of the Boot CPU of a Large Web App   In production, the...
articles.body_html:
How I Cut 60% of the Bundle and 76% of the Boot CPU of a Large Web App

In production, the home page of the app took more than 10 seconds. Now it takes under 1 second.

No single trick did that. I cut the JavaScript and CSS that every page downloads from 6,070 KB to 2,434 KB gzip, and the code that runs before the first paint from 6.1 s to 1.5 s of CPU. I moved more than 1,000 templates out of the main bundle and loaded each one with its route. Then I served the lazy code from a CDN I designed, in chunks built from the module graph.

In this article I'll walk through how I found where the time went, the tools I built to measure it, each cut with its numbers, the lazy-loading patterns I kept, the traps that broke features, and what the CDN changed.

The case: a large web app with about 1,150 client templates, React panels inside them, and about 9,000 lazy modules. It runs on Meteor 2.16. Some limitations of this work come from Meteor, and I'll name them. The method does not depend on Meteor.

The Result

Home page in production Before After
Time until the page starts to show 12.6 s 0.8 s

I measured the "after" number in production, after the CDN release, logged in: 0.89 s at the median of five loads.

The other numbers in this article come from the lab, and they are higher than the production number. That is expected. The lab starts every load with an empty cache, so the browser downloads and compiles all the code each time. It runs on a local server, with no CDN and no HTTP/2. Its timings count until the largest element of the page appears. A second lab profile also slows the network to Fast 3G and the CPU by 4x, close to what a slow phone gets. I used the lab only to compare two versions of the code with the same test.

What every page downloads. The measurement is deterministic, so these numbers are exact.

Eager bundle, gzip Start End Change
JavaScript 5,666 KB 2,042 KB −64.0%
JavaScript + CSS 6,070 KB 2,434 KB −59.9%

A cold load of /home in the lab. Median of five loads. I measured both columns on the same day.

Measurement Start After the view tree Change
Modules in the main bundle 11,177 5,041 −54.9%
CPU spent running modules before the first paint 6,113 ms 1,454 ms −76.2% (4.2x)
Longest task 6,476 ms 2,053 ms −68.3% (3.2x)
First Contentful Paint 8,704 ms 2,900 ms −66.7% (3.0x)
Largest Contentful Paint 8,988 ms 4,068 ms −54.7% (2.2x)
LCP, 5 core routes, one load each 9.6–10.8 s 3.9–4.8 s −53% to −62%

The timings come from the view-tree commit. Three later cuts took another 352 KB gzip out of the JavaScript, and I did not measure their timings in the lab. The bundle table includes them.

Where the Time Went

Before I had a profile, I did two rounds of bundle work: the error-tracking SDK, a second copy of pdf.js, a timezone library, and a few feature routes. They took 622 KB gzip out of the JavaScript. On Fast 3G with a 4x slower CPU, the median LCP of the five core routes fell by 11 s. On localhost, the LCP of /home went from 8,684 to 8,172 ms, and the ranges of the two builds overlapped. Fewer bytes helped the slow network. They did not shorten the wait on a fast one.

So I measured where the time went. The first runtime measurement was a timeline of one cold load of /home, on the build after those two rounds:

Moment Time
The HTML arrives 21 ms
The CSS arrives 181 ms
The JavaScript (5,043 KB gzip, 23,189 KB raw) downloads 59–1,322 ms
One long task: the bundle parses and runs 1,432–6,747 ms
The WebSocket opens 6,878 ms
First Contentful Paint 6,884 ms
Largest Contentful Paint 7,724 ms

On the five core routes of that build, the LCP was 7.7 to 9.8 s, and the shape was the same on every route. The network delivered the bundle in 1.3 s. Then the tab spent 5.3 s in one long task, with nothing on the screen. The first paint came 6 ms after that task ended. No data request could start before it, because the code that opens the socket was inside the same bundle.

Two more numbers explained the size of the problem:

  • Only a third of the code ran. V8 coverage on /home showed 7.7 MB of the 23.1 MB of eager JavaScript in use. The browser downloaded and decompressed the other 15.4 MB, and V8 still pre-parsed it, but none of it ran.
  • A slow network made it extreme. On Fast 3G with a 4x slower CPU, the LCP of the five core routes was 51 to 55 s.

So the problem had two parts: too many bytes, and too much CPU at boot. They turned out to be separate problems, with separate fixes.

Measure First: Three Small Tools

The usual tools gave me wrong answers, so I wrote three small scripts.

1. Exact bytes per module. A bundle visualizer that reads the source map puts the bytes of generated code (the compiled templates, for example) on a neighboring file, because the map has no entry for them. measureEagerBundle.js parses the module tree of the built bundle instead, so each module gets its exact byte span. It is deterministic: two builds of the same code give the same numbers.

2. CPU per module. A sampling profile said that one file, the one that creates the app's 112 database collections, cost 2,160 ms. That was wrong. The profile reads positions through the same source map. measureModuleTime.js replaces the module installer before the bundle runs and wraps every module function with a timer. The real cost of that file was about 280 ms. This is the core of it, simplified:

// Runs before the bundle (Playwright addInitScript).
// Meteor gives every module tree to one global installer.
// The hook wraps each module function with a timer.
const stack = [];
window.__moduleTimes = [];

function wrapTree(tree, prefix) {
  const out = Array.isArray(tree) ? [] : {};
  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(tree)) {
    const modulePath = prefix ? `${prefix}/${key}` : key;
    if (typeof value !== 'function') {
      out[key] = value && typeof value === 'object' ? wrapTree(value, modulePath) : value;
      continue;
    }
    out[key] = function timedModule(...args) {
      const frame = { child: 0 };
      stack.push(frame);
      const started = performance.now();
      try {
        return value.apply(this, args);
      } finally {
        const elapsed = performance.now() - started;
        stack.pop();
        // The parent's own time does not include the time of its children.
        if (stack.length) stack[stack.length - 1].child += elapsed;
        window.__moduleTimes.push({ path: modulePath, self: elapsed - frame.child });
      }
    };
  }
  return out;
}

let wrapped;
Object.defineProperty(window, 'meteorInstall', {
  configurable: true,
  get: () => wrapped,
  set(realInstall) {
    wrapped = (tree, options) => realInstall(wrapTree(tree, ''), options);
    Object.assign(wrapped, realInstall);
  },
});

No source map is involved. One rule made the report useful: a large number means "this module is the door to an expensive package". npm packages go through a separate copy of the installer, so they have no row of their own. Their cost goes to the first app module that requires them.

3. The doors. edges.js walks the static import graph from every file that loads on every page, and stops at each dynamic import(). It answers two questions: which npm packages a page can reach, and which eager file is the first import on the chain to a module. I call that file a door. Close the door, and everything behind it leaves the bundle.

node scripts/perf/edges.js "$PWD" npm:material-react-table   # the eager importers of one package
node scripts/perf/edges.js "$PWD" <directory>                # the chains that reach a folder

For page timings, one run was useless. Five cold loads of the same build varied by up to 940 ms on localhost. I took the median of five loads per side, and I used Fast 3G with a slower CPU when I needed to separate two results.

The Cuts, One Door at a Time

First, every step on one table. The bytes are exact. The timings are cold loads of /home on the same machine, with the same script and the same account.

Step Eager JS, gzip Saved Module evaluation Longest task LCP
Start 5,666 KB — 6,113 ms 6,476 ms 8,988 ms
1. Error-tracking SDK, second pdf.js, timezone library, feature routes 5,044 KB −622 KB 5,319 ms 5,772 ms 8,172 ms
2. Video recorder 5,014 KB −30 KB 4,290 ms 4,438 ms 7,028 ms
3. Table library 4,712 KB −302 KB 3,516 ms 3,534 ms 5,708 ms
4. Server code, date pickers, AI chat panels 4,496 KB −216 KB 2,712 ms 3,364 ms 5,828 ms
5. Content catalogue, video-call SDK 4,398 KB −164 KB¹ — 3,457 ms² 5,716 ms²
6. View tree 2,394 KB −2,004 KB³ 1,454 ms 2,053 ms 4,068 ms
7. Server-only reporting helpers 2,345 KB −49 KB — — —
8. Material UI off the first paint 2,107 KB −238 KB — — —
9. jQuery UI 2,042 KB −65 KB — — —

¹ A merge of new code from the main branch added 66 KB between steps 4 and 5, so the column moves by 98 KB, not 164 KB.
² Median of three loads. The other LCP and longest-task cells are medians of five.
³ Step 6 holds 24 commits. The move of the view tree is the largest.

I measured the start row and step 6 on the same day. I measured steps 1 to 5 on two earlier days, when the start build had an LCP of 8,684 ms. Read the timing columns as a trend, and the byte column as exact. The table counts JavaScript only. Step 1 also cut the CSS from 404 KB to 271 KB, a revert of that CSS work came back with step 6, and the CSS is now 392 KB.

Two things stand out. Step 2 saved 30 KB and took 1 s off the boot CPU. Step 6 saved 2 MB, more than all the other steps together.

Before the profile: an error-tracking SDK (step 1)

The bundler cannot tree-shake, so a static import of @sentry/browser brought the SDK with replay, feedback and canvas recording: 916 KB minified. Twelve client files imported it.

I made one module the only door. It queues every call, and it loads the SDK in requestIdleCallback after the first route paints, with a 4 s limit. Errors raised before that go into a 20-entry buffer and reach Sentry when it starts. The Sentry packages left the bundle: −276 KB gzip.

A recorder that cost 1 second of CPU (step 2)

The CPU report put one module at the top: the app's video recorder component, at 1,032 ms. It was the first file to require react-media-recorder, which pulls standardized-audio-context. That library builds a class hierarchy when it loads. It is cheap to download and expensive to run.

Exactly one eager file imported the recorder, for a panel that renders behind a condition. I made that import lazy:

Cold load of /home, median of 5 Before After
FCP 7,276 ms 6,256 ms (−14.0%)
LCP 8,172 ms 7,028 ms (−14.0%)
Longest task 5,772 ms 4,438 ms (−23.1%)

The bundle barely moved: 5,044 KB to 5,014 KB gzip. Boot CPU and bundle size are separate problems. A byte budget alone would never have found this.

A table library behind 22 doors (step 3)

The next module was the app's table wrapper, at 795 ms, the door to material-react-table. Making that one file lazy did not help: 37 modules imported the package, through 22 different doors. Most of them were template helpers that returned a React component at module scope. Each one became a lazy component.

Result: −302 KB gzip, −774 ms of module evaluation. After the recorder and the table, the longest task on /home was 42.7% shorter than at the start.

Server code that ran in the browser (step 4)

Shared code had if (Meteor.isClient) return; at the top, but it still imported the server's event store. Those modules built a validation schema when they loaded: 234 ms of CPU in the browser, for code that never runs there. A function-level require() stopped the CPU cost, but the bundler still found the literal and kept the bytes.

The fix that removes the bytes too is a registry: the shared code has an empty slot, and a server-only file fills it.

// Shared code: the slot.
let eventStore: EventStore | null = null;

export function registerEventStore(store: EventStore): void {
  eventStore = store;
}

export function getEventStore(): EventStore {
  if (!eventStore) {
    throw new Error('The event store is not registered.');
  }
  return eventStore;
}

// server/registerEventStore.ts: the only import of the real module.
registerEventStore({ append });

A catalogue that the header loaded for one field (step 5)

The header called a hook, the hook called a helper, and the helper read a content catalogue of 43 items with all their text. It used one field of each item: the _id.

I moved the 43 ids to a small file, and I kept the full catalogue lazy. A unit test compares the two lists, so a new item that reaches only one file fails the build. Result: −160 KB gzip, and a feature folder fell from 60 eager modules to 12.

A video-call SDK that loaded on every page (step 5)

The chat panel sits in the default layout, and its onCreated hook loaded the video-call SDK: an 843 KB gzip chunk, on every page, for every user. Nobody had started a call.

Now the SDK loads when a chat window holds a live video. For one screen that needs it right after a click, the download starts at the click, while the modal opens and the server creates the session. 843 KB gzip stopped loading on every page.

Smaller doors

Door What it cost
A date picker package imported through its root barrel 73 KB gzip, 260 ms of CPU across 3 files
AI chat panels in 5 template helpers the door to a charting library, 97 KB gzip
A PDF viewer package that listed pdf.js twice 406 KB minified, one copy ran and exported nothing
moment-timezone from npm next to a global moment 763 KB minified, for one component

The big one: templates that load with their route (step 6)

Each fix above closed one door. The bundle was still about 4.4 MB gzip, because the framework loads every file under client/ on every page, whatever the imports say. More than 1,000 templates lived there.

The key observation: the templating layer finds a template by name when it renders, not when the file loads. So a route can wait for a chunk, and then render any template inside it. Only the templates that render on every page must load with the page: 135 of 1,148.

I moved the view tree to a lazy folder. A list of 155 files loads with the page. The other 604 files load in a route chunk. Each route group waits for its chunk:

const adminArea = createRouteChunkLoader({
  importChunk: () => import('/imports/features/admin/ui'),
});

const adminRoutes = FlowRouter.group({
  name: 'adminRoutes',
  waitOn: adminArea.waitOn,
  whileWaiting: adminArea.whileWaiting,
});

The helper exists for one reason. The router calls whileWaiting on every route run, and a query parameter change is a route run. A plain waitOn showed the loading screen on each change, so the page lost its state. The helper shows the loading screen only while the chunk is on the way.

This table compares the start with step 6:

Measurement Start After the view tree
Eager JavaScript, gzip 5,666 KB 2,394 KB (−57.8%)
Modules in the bundle 11,177 5,041 (−54.9%)
npm packages that a page can reach 57 40
Module evaluation on /home 6,113 ms 1,454 ms (−76.2%)
Longest task on /home 6,476 ms 2,053 ms (−68.3%)
LCP on /home, median of 5 8,988 ms 4,068 ms (−54.7%)
Share of the eager code that runs on /home 34.6% 50.2%

On the five core routes, LCP fell between 53% and 62% in the lab, and between 42% and 46% on Fast 3G with a 4x slower CPU. The longest task fell between 68% and 75%.

Three more doors after the view tree (steps 7 to 9)

  • Reporting helpers that only the server calls. 48 files moved to a server folder, which never enters the client bundle: −49 KB gzip.
  • Material UI on the first paint. Four static imports still carried it: a barrel file of the component library that 37 files read for the theme, the entry of the confirmation dialog, a menu with its own table, and a demo page. The barrel went away. The dialog entry now loads the dialog on its first call, so its 131 call sites did not change. Result: −238 KB gzip, and the Material UI components in the bundle fell from 73 to 33. The 33 that stay belong to the header, which paints on every page.
  • jQuery UI. The file (247 KB raw) sat in an eager folder, and no file on the first-paint path called a widget. It moved to a lazy folder, and the 67 modules that call a widget import it: −65 KB gzip.

After the Bundle: the Data Waterfall

A smaller bundle moved the first paint earlier, and then the data became visible. After the long task, the page opened its socket and sent 28 subscriptions for 109 documents. The payload was small. The cost was the number of round trips and their order.

Only 3 of the 28 held the first paint. That fact told me which fixes would move LCP and which would not:

  • Duplicate subscriptions. Two call sites asked for the same data, so the server ran two publications twice. I gave each subscription one owner: 28 became 26. LCP did not move. I had predicted that, because the duplicates did not hold the paint. The page still did less work.
  • A 3-second timer from 2018. Six subscriptions waited for a setTimeout of 3,000 ms that no longer had a purpose. They held 80 of the 109 documents. Without the timer, notifications were ready 506 ms after the first subscription message, instead of 3,042 ms. LCP did not move here either: none of the six held the paint.
  • A blocking waitOn. / and /home waited for a full publication before they rendered anything, and the same data was already on its way through another subscription. I removed the wait.
  • A publication that read a whole user document. One of the 3 that hold the paint read the full user document, which grows with every login session, to get one field. With a projection it went from 126 ms to 18 ms. The 3 run in parallel, so the gate went from 126 ms to 56 ms, a gain too small for the lab to show in LCP.

Cutting requests that do not hold the paint does not move LCP. Find the requests that do, and make them shorter.

Patterns I Kept

A React panel that loads on its first render 

// Rendered only when its panel opens, so it loads on demand.
const SecurityPanelLazy = lazyComponent(
  () => import('/imports/features/account/ui/SecurityPanel'),
  'SecurityPanel',
);

lazyComponent shows a spinner until the module arrives. When the download fails, it renders nothing, reports the failure, and shows a toast that offers a reload.

Code that runs after a click 

'click button[data-action="create-project"]'(event, template) {
  // The handler stays synchronous: the template layer drops the promise
  // of an async handler, so a failed chunk would leave the button dead.
  import('/imports/features/projects/ui/CreateProjectDialog')
    .then(({ showCreateProjectDialog }) => showCreateProjectDialog(userId))
    .catch(error => {
      reportError(error, { context: 'CreateProjectDialogLoadFailed' });
    });
},

A library that loads at the moment of use 

let chartPromise;

export const loadChart = () => {
  if (!chartPromise) {
    chartPromise = import('chart.js').then(({ default: Chart }) => {
      Chart.defaults.global.pointHitDetectionRadius = 1;
      return Chart;
    });
    // A failed download clears the promise, so the next chart tries again.
    chartPromise = chartPromise.catch(error => {
      chartPromise = undefined;
      throw error;
    });
  }
  return chartPromise;
};

Every caller waits for the same download, and the global setup of the library runs once. After the await, check that the component still exists.

A small index of large data

Keep the part that eager code reads in a small eager file, keep the full data lazy, and add a test that fails when the two differ. I used this for the content catalogue and for a list of program definitions.

Traps That Broke Features

A lazy load changes when code runs. Each of these broke a feature during the work:

  • A side-effect module stopped running. A file that registers custom validators moved to a lazy folder, and only the server imported it. Eight forms failed validation with Expected undefined, got string.
  • A global stopped existing. Seven files assigned helpers to a global namespace and moved with no importer. Creating a form failed with ... is not a function.
  • The CSS cascade changed. A lazy stylesheet loads last, so its rules win. One component stylesheet imported the global styles and restyled every button.
  • A route waited for its own chunk. A redirect module sat inside the chunk that waits for a route, and the route waited for the redirect module. The page stayed on the loading screen.
  • Two modules changed order. Both read a value that clears when it is read. A deep link after a login landed on the home page.
  • A pre-commit hook rewrote a vendor file. eslint --fix changed var to let in a minified jQuery UI file, and every view that used it failed to load.
  • A moved file left an import on the old path. Neither ESLint nor the build reported it. The browser threw Cannot find module only when the import ran.

The last one is the most dangerous, because nothing fails before production. I test every changed page three ways: a cold deep link in a private window, a hard reload, and an in-app navigation, then again on Fast 3G.

The CDN

Lazy loading moved cost from boot to navigation. After the view tree left the bundle, /home asked for its route code in one request to the app server: 1,021 KB, between the first paint at 2,900 ms and the LCP at 4,068 ms. The same request had a second problem. After a deploy, the server answered with the code of its new build, so an open tab could receive modules from another build.

I moved the lazy modules to a CDN with versioned names, so every tab reads the modules of its own build. The full design will be in my next article. These are the parts that matter for speed:

  • Chunks from the module graph. The first version made one request per module. /home needs 2,591 lazy modules, so it made about 2,600 requests. In a sandbox, a public route with about 2,000 modules took 9.4 to 9.9 s through CloudFront, against 1.7 to 2.1 s through the app server. So I grouped the modules with the rules of Rollup, webpack and Turbopack. On a production build, /home now loads its 2,591 modules in 24 chunks, plus one index. The chunks carry 1.0% more bytes than the modules that /home needs.
  • A cache per module. Meteor's dynamic-import package already stores each module in IndexedDB under its version. With the CDN, that cache holds only modules of the right build. A second visit to the same build makes one request: the index of the build.
  • Small deploys stay small. After a deploy, the browser plans each chunk: it downloads the whole chunk only when the requests that it saves cost more than its unused bytes. The modules that did not change come from the local cache.
  • Edges and HTTP/2. CloudFront serves the chunks from an edge near the user, with Brotli and up to 128 parallel streams on one connection.
  • A preload that I removed. Preloading the chunks from the HTML gained 0.31 s, and cost about 12 s when the preload failed.

Not in production yet. A 30 s total timeout per request aborted the largest chunk of /home (4.3 MB before compression) on a 3G profile while its data was still arriving. The fix aborts a request only after 10 s with no data on any CDN request.

Keeping It Fast

A bundle that shrinks by 60% grows back if nobody watches it. So I wrote down 13 ways the bundle grew back, each with an example from the app's history: a new file in an eager folder, one static import into a large tree, a barrel import, a download from code that runs on every page, server code in shared folders, large data in an eager file, a second copy of a library, generated CSS, and others.

The contribution rules of the project now point to this list. A change that adds a file to an eager folder, or a dependency to client code, starts with a read of it. A release gate in CI also measures the JavaScript that / downloads on a staging server, and it fails above a budget of 2,042 KiB.

The Limitations

  • Lab and production are different setups. The lab numbers come from localhost with an empty cache and no CDN. The production "after" number is my own measurement for a returning user, on one account and one machine, not a p75 of all users.
  • A first visit to a route waits for its chunk. Lazy loading moves cost from boot to navigation. A failed chunk needs a recovery path, and every page needs a test on a slow network.
  • Meteor 2 loads every file under client/ and both/ on every page. The meteor.mainModule option turns that off, and this app does not use it. In an app of this size, every file needs an importer before that option can work, which is the same work as the view-tree move. There is no tree shaking either, so every cut needed a move, not only an import().
  • A require() inside a function still bundles the module. The bundler reads the literal. Only a registry slot removes the bytes.
  • Each lazy chunk grows the version manifest. The main bundle carries the version of every lazy module. It grew from 152 KB to 556 KB raw during this work, and it is now 288 KB gzip, 14% of the eager JavaScript.
  • Some weight is still on every page. The header keeps 33 Material UI components, 128 KB gzip of Material UI in all. The icon font stylesheet blocks the first render, and /home downloads 453 KB of fonts. About 495 method stubs in a shared folder still reach the browser.
  • The home chunk is still large. /home asks for the chunk of the whole authenticated area, not only for the templates that it renders.

Conclusion

In production, the home page went from more than 10 seconds to under 1 second for a returning user. In the lab, the same work cut 60% of the bytes and 76% of the boot CPU. These are the lessons I keep:

  • Measure bytes and CPU separately. A 1 s CPU cost hid behind a library that was cheap to download.
  • Find the doors, not the files. One static import from an eager file can bring a whole package. Close the door, and the package leaves.
  • Build your own measurements when the usual tools are wrong. Source maps put bytes and CPU on the wrong files. Five runs per side, not one.
  • The large win was structural. The fixes to single doors saved tens to hundreds of KB each. Moving the view tree to its routes saved about 2 MB gzip.
  • Fix what holds the paint. Requests that do not hold the first paint do not move LCP.
  • Give the lazy code a short path too. Versioned chunks on a CDN, a cache that matches the build, and a few well-sized requests.
  • Guard it. A written list of the known regressions and a budget in CI keep the bundle where you left it.

articles.title: Ghost of Rates Past: your old mortgage rate comes back to warn you
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine    ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

In 2020 and 2021 a lot of Canadians locked in five-year fixed mortgage rates at historic lows. Those terms are ending now. The Bank of Canada estimated that people with a five-year fixed mortgage renewing in 2026 would see their payment go up about 20% on average.

That rate was a quiet thing. It came out of your account every month and you stopped noticing it. Then the term ends and it's gone.

So for Halloween I let it come back as a ghost.

Ghost of Rates Past asks for four things: when you signed, how much you borrowed, the rate you got, and the renewal rate you've been offered. It works out what happens to your payment, shows you the Bank of Canada's posted rate the week you signed next to the one today, and then your old rate writes you a short letter:

I've lingered here, a steady hum within your walls for a long time now. I was the small, quiet payment that flowed monthly, a constant reassurance. I've faded, haven't I?

I was born in 2021 at 1.89%. While I lived, your payment was $2,091 a month. At renewal in 2026, the rate waiting for you is 4.39%. Your payment becomes $2,610 a month: $519 more, or $6,231 more a year.

Do not wait for the letter in the mail. Start comparing lenders early, and read the renewal offer closely.

— your old rate

(A real letter from a test run. Example numbers: $500,000 borrowed, 25-year amortization, 1.89% in March 2021, renewing at 4.39%.)

The spooky part is written by an open-weight model running in your own browser. The numbers are not.

Demo

Live: https://alenzacodes.github.io/ghost-of-rates-past/

Open it, press Summon. The first time, your browser downloads the model once (about 760 MB with WebGPU) and keeps it. If your browser can't run it, untick the model box and you'll get the plain letter with the same numbers.

Code

ALENZACODES / ghost-of-rates-past

Your old mortgage rate comes back as a ghost to warn you before renewal. Runs Gemma 3 1B in your browser; numbers from plain, tested JavaScript.

👻 Ghost of Rates Past

Your old mortgage rate comes back to warn you before renewal.

Many Canadians locked in a low 5-year fixed rate in 2020 or 2021 and are renewing now. Type in the rate you signed and the renewal rate you've been offered. The page works out what happens to your payment, and the ghost of your old rate writes you a short letter about it.

The letter's spooky opening is written by Gemma 3 1B, an open-weight model, running in your browser with Transformers.js. Your numbers never leave your device. There is no server and no API key.

Made in Toronto, Ontario for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine. Started Oct 30, 2026.

The one rule: the ghost never touches the numbers

Small models are bad at numbers. When I gave the model the figures and asked…

View on GitHub

It's a static site: index.html, about 240 lines of JavaScript, a small JSON file of Bank of Canada rate data, and tests. No build step, no server, no API keys.

How I Built It

The model: Gemma 3 1B instruct, using the ONNX build from onnx-community.

The runtime: Transformers.js loads it straight from a CDN and runs it on WebGPU when the browser has it, and on the CPU (WASM) when it doesn't.

const adapter = navigator.gpu ? await navigator.gpu.requestAdapter().catch(() => null) : null;
const device = adapter ? 'webgpu' : 'wasm';
generator = await pipeline('text-generation', 'onnx-community/gemma-3-1b-it-ONNX', {
  dtype: device === 'webgpu' ? 'q4f16' : 'q4',
  device,
});

The math: plain JavaScript in calc.js. Fixed mortgage rates in Canada are compounded semi-annually, so the monthly rate is (1 + r/2)^(1/6) - 1, not r/12. A test checks it against the textbook case: $100,000 at 5% over 25 years is $581.60 a month.

The part I learned the most from: the ghost isn't allowed to touch the numbers.

My first version gave Gemma all the figures and asked it to write the whole letter. I ran it a bunch of times on my own machine. With a list of facts in the prompt, it just copied the list back to me (10 out of 10 times). When I asked it to rewrite a plain letter in a ghost's voice instead, the writing got better, but none of 6 tries kept every number right. It left out the $519 increase, which is the whole point. One letter said "$2,610 a year" when it's a month. In my very first test it turned 1.89% into 2.09%.

For a tool about someone's mortgage, a confident wrong number is the scariest thing on the page. So I split the job:

Part of the letter Written by
Payments, balance, difference calc.js, unit tested
The eerie opening Gemma 3 1B, in your browser
The practical nudge fixed text

The model is never shown a single number, and guard.js checks what comes back:

export function check(text) {
  const numbers = findNumbers(text);                 // any digit, or words like "twenty", "half", "percent"
  const tooLong = text.split(/[.!?]+\s/).length > 5;
  const empty = text.trim().length < 40;
  const placeholder = /[\[\]{}<>]|---/.test(text);   // "[Recipient's Name]" happened once
  return { pass: numbers.length === 0 && !tooLong && !empty && !placeholder, numbers, tooLong, empty, placeholder };
}

If an attempt fails, it's thrown out and the ghost tries again, up to three times, and then the page falls back to a plain opening. Small models also stop mid-sentence when they hit the token limit, so tidy() keeps whole sentences only, three at most, and drops "Dearest you," style greeting lines. With the final prompt, 10 out of 10 test runs on my own machine passed the guard on the first try. An earlier prompt passed 8 of 10, and the two misses ran long, so the guard and retry still earn their place.

The result: the model does what it's good at (mood), and plain code does what it's good at (arithmetic).

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Because of what people type into it. Your mortgage balance, your rate and the date you bought your home are private. With an open-weight model running in the browser, none of it goes to anyone's server. Mine included. There is no backend to leak and no log to keep.

It also costs nothing to run. A closed API would mean a key, a bill and rate limits for a free Halloween tool. Here the cost is one download on the visitor's side, and after that the model is cached and runs on their own device.

And it will still work later. Free tools tend to disappear when the service behind them shuts down or changes its pricing. This one is a folder of static files plus a model anyone can download. If a host disappears, you can run it from your own laptop with python3 -m http.server.

Open weights also made the guard possible to test properly. I could run the exact same model on my own machine, as many times as I wanted, to see how it fails before shipping.

The Spirit of It

Día de los Muertos is about remembering what's gone without pretending it isn't. That felt like the right frame for a renewal. The low rate isn't coming back. The ghost isn't there to scare you; it's there so you see the new number months early, while you still have time to shop around, instead of on the day the renewal letter shows up.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma

Built in Toronto, Ontario. Thanks for reading. If you renewed recently, I'd like to hear whether the letter matched what you saw.

articles.title: I built a bookmarklet that shows where the Tab key goes, and what it never reaches
articles.description: Tab trail draws every Tab stop on any page and marks in red what fails WCAG 2.2 AA. 1 file, MIT, works in your Playwright tests too.
articles.body_html:
Run Lighthouse on any page and scroll to the bottom of the Accessibility section. There is a list called "Additional items to manually check". Two of them are about the keyboard: "Interactive controls are keyboard focusable" and "The page has a logical tab order".

Manually. I wanted to check every page of my own site with the keyboard, so I built a tool for it.

What it is

Tab trail is a bookmarklet. Click it on any page and it draws a numbered dot on every Tab stop, joined by a line in the order the keyboard visits them. The stop you are on turns orange. Press Tab and follow the numbers, or press Play and it walks every stop for you.

Then it marks in red what fails WCAG 2.2 AA.

Try it on the live page. It has 3 things broken on purpose, so the first click shows red.

What turns red

7 checks, each with its WCAG rule:

  • Missed spots (2.1.1 A). Something looks clickable (a pointer cursor, a button role, an onclick) but Tab never gets there. The classic <div onClick> "Add to cart".
  • Hover menus (2.1.1 A, 2.4.7 AA). A menu that opens on :hover but never when Tab reaches it.
  • Forced order (2.4.3 A). A tabindex="5" that pulls an element ahead of the rest of the page.
  • Hidden focus (2.4.11 AA). Tab lands on something a sticky header, cookie bar or chat button covers completely. This one is new in WCAG 2.2.
  • Keyboard trap (2.1.2 A). Tab and Shift+Tab both leave focus on the same spot.
  • Lost focus (2.4.3 A). A popup closes and focus drops to the top of the page instead of going back to the button that opened it.
  • Out of order (2.4.3 A). Tab jumps somewhere it shouldn't, or a popup that blocks the page doesn't get Tab first.

The parts that were harder than they look

Hover menus come from CSS, so it reads your CSS. It goes through every style sheet it can read for :hover rules that show something (display, visibility, opacity, max-height) that is hidden right now and holds a link or button. Then it looks for a :focus, :focus-within or :focus-visible rule that shows the same element. No match and no aria-expanded toggle means red. Nested CSS and Tailwind v4 output had to work too: & rules resolved against their parent, @media inside rules, :hover inside :is() and :where().

Hidden focus needs the page to stop moving. After each Tab press it waits until scrolling is done, then tests 5 points on the focused element (the center and 4 corners). Only when all 5 land on something fixed or sticky is it flagged. Partly covered passes AA, so it is not red.

Safari and Firefox on a Mac skip links on Tab by default. Safari skips links and buttons until you turn on "Press Tab to highlight each item", Firefox skips links until you turn on Keyboard navigation in System Settings. A naive checker would flag every one of those presses as a jump. Tab trail marks them SKIPPED and tells you which setting to flip.

It has to survive any site. It draws inside its own shadow root, so the page's CSS can't touch it. It runs under a strict Content Security Policy and Trusted Types. When the page opens a modal <dialog>, everything outside it goes inert, so the tool moves itself into the dialog to stay clickable and moves back out when it closes.

Firefox can't store it. A bookmark there can be at most 65,536 characters, and Tab trail is 223,286. In Firefox you paste the script in the console.

Hand it to your AI

"Copy for AI" copies only the problems, each with its WCAG rule, what should happen, a unique CSS selector, a trimmed HTML snippet, the React, Vue or Angular component that drew it (on a dev build), a fix hint and how to check the fix. Paste it into your coding agent and it knows where to look.

Long numbers, emails and things that look like tokens are masked before they reach your clipboard. Read it once anyway.

Put it in your tests

While it is open, the page has window.__tabTrail, so a test can run it with no clicks:

npm i -D --save-exact tab-trail

import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

const script = readFileSync("node_modules/tab-trail/dist/tab-trail.js", "utf8");

test("Tab reaches everything", async ({ page }) => {
  test.setTimeout(300_000);
  await page.goto("http://localhost:5173/");
  await page.evaluate(script);
  await page.evaluate(() => window.__tabTrail.play());
  const problems = await page.evaluate(() => window.__tabTrail.problems());
  expect(problems.map((p) => `${p.check}: ${p.selector}`)).toEqual([]);
});

play() moves focus through every stop, so it covers Missed spots, Hover menus, Forced order and Hidden focus. Out of order and Keyboard trap need real Tab and Shift+Tab presses, and state().untested tells you which checks never ran, so a green test can tell a clean page from a skipped check. The full example, with the TypeScript types, is in the README.

Already run axe? Keep it. axe reads the HTML, Tab trail walks the Tab key.

What it doesn't do

It's the keyboard part, not a full audit. It checks that Tab gets there, not that Enter or Space then works. It doesn't compare Tab order with the visual order when CSS moves things around, doesn't judge your focus ring's contrast, and doesn't tell you what a screen reader says. Style sheets from other domains without CORS can't be read. The whole list is in docs/limits.md, and how it sits next to Accessibility Insights, WAVE and the rest is in docs/compared.md.

It reads the page and sends nothing: no network requests, no cookies, no storage. Close it and it's gone.

Get it

matjazkorosec / tab-trail

Tab order and focus order checker. A bookmarklet that draws every Tab stop and marks what Tab never reaches. WCAG 2.2 AA check helper.

Tab trail

One click shows the path the Tab key takes through any page, and marks in red what fails WCAG 2.2 AA.

Some people only use the keyboard. If Tab skips your "Add to cart" button, they can't buy from you. If it skips "Send" on your contact form, they can't write to you. Even Lighthouse tells you to check this by hand. Tab trail checks it for you.

I built it to check every page of my own site with the keyboard. Try it on the live page, it has 3 things broken on purpose.

Install

Bookmark

  1. Open matjazkorosec.com/tools/tab-trail and drag the Tab trail button to your bookmarks bar. Don't see the bookmarks bar? Press Ctrl+Shift+B, or Cmd+Shift+B on a Mac.
  2. Open your site and click the bookmark.
  3. Press Tab and follow the numbers, or press Play and it walks every stop for you. Click the bookmark…
View on GitHub

1 file of plain JavaScript, MIT licensed. Drag the button from the page to your bookmarks bar, click it on your own site, and press Play.

If it gets something wrong on your site, press Copy log in the panel and open an issue with it. I'd like to see the pages that break it.

articles.title: Googlebot ran my analytics script — my unique visitor count was 14x too high
articles.description: My dashboard said 87 visitors. The real number was 6. Googlebot renders JavaScript, fires the beacon, and crawls from dozens of egress IPs — so every page it fetches looks like a new visitor. Four checks that separate machines from people.
articles.body_html:
For three weeks, my site's dashboard told a nice story. Traffic was growing. Unique visitors hit 87 on the best day, then 94, then a hundred-odd. New site, indexing starting to happen, numbers going up — exactly what you want to see.

Then I looked at the actual requests and found six humans.

Not six hundred. Six. And two of those six were probably me.

This post is about where the other 81 came from, why the usual bot filters miss them, and the four checks that finally made the number honest. If you run a small site with a hand-rolled analytics endpoint, you have the same problem — you just don't know it yet.

The mechanism: rendered pages run JavaScript

I built the analytics myself. A tiny script posts to /api/pv on page load; a Cloudflare Worker writes a row into D1 with path, referrer, UA, and IP. Fifty lines, no vendor, no cookie banner.

That design assumes a visit is a person. It isn't.

Googlebot fetches a page, renders it in headless Chromium, and executes the JavaScript — my beacon included. So every page Google crawls generates a "visit". On a 380-page site, one crawl pass is up to 380 hits. And because crawlers don't reuse a connection the way a browser session does, each batch can arrive from a different egress IP, so COUNT(DISTINCT ip) treats them as hundreds of separate people.

That's the whole illusion. Nothing was broken. My endpoint correctly recorded what happened. It just recorded the wrong thing as a visitor.

Worth knowing the scale before you go hunting: on my site, Googlebot had crawled 372 of 380 pages, while bingbot had crawled 5. Both are "search engine traffic" in a naive dashboard. One of them is 70x the other, and neither is a person.

Fix attempt #1: filter on user agent (insufficient)

The obvious move — classify at ingest time, store the result, and never reinterpret it later:

const UA_BOT = /bot|crawl|spider|slurp|headless|phantom|puppeteer|playwright|selenium|curl\/|wget|python-|go-http-client|java\/|okhttp|axios|node-fetch|scrapy|semrush|ahrefs|dataforseo|lighthouse/i;

function classifyUA(ua) {
  const s = String(ua || '').slice(0, 200);
  if (!s) return '?';
  if (UA_BOT.test(s)) return 'bot';
  if (/ipad|tablet|silk\//i.test(s)) return 'tb';
  if (/android|iphone|mobile/i.test(s)) return 'mb';
  return 'pc';
}

This caught the honest bots immediately — Googlebot, bingbot, AhrefsBot. It also caught a few things I hadn't thought of:

  • GoogleOther, Google-InspectionTool, APIs-Google, FeedFetcher — Google's non-search fetchers. A regex containing only bot misses all of them.
  • BuiltWith, DataForSEO, Lighthouse — audit tools that behave exactly like a crawler.
  • HeadlessChrome — the giveaway inside otherwise-normal Chrome UAs.

The mediapartners and google-inspectiontool entries were the ones that actually moved my numbers. Add them even if you've never heard of them.

But UA filtering alone fails on two cases, and both were present on my site.

The case that fooled me three times: fake WeChat traffic

I kept seeing a cluster of "WeChat" visitors. Mobile, from Tencent Cloud IP ranges, hundreds of hits. On a Chinese-language engineering site, WeChat referrals are the single most plausible traffic source, so I believed it — three separate times, over three weeks, before I stopped believing it.

What finally exposed it:

Mozilla/5.0 (Linux; Android 5.1; Nexus 5 Build/MRA58N) AppleWebKit/537.36
(KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/74.0.3729.131 Mobile Safari/537.36
MicroMessenger/7.0.1

Three independent tells:

  1. MicroMessenger/7.0.1 — that's a 2018 client. Real WeChat traffic in 2026 reports 8.x and carries a build identifier like (0x28002d3a). A version with no (0x segment is not the real client.
  2. Nexus 5 Build/MRA58N — that is Puppeteer's default device descriptor, straight out of the library's device list. Real Android devices in the wild report their own build string.
  3. Tencent Cloud IP ranges — 81.71., 183.60., 42.194., 14.152., 43.248. are datacenter, not mobile carriers.

A single tell is weak. Three together is conclusive. The lesson generalises: a UA string is a claim, not evidence. Check whether the claim is internally consistent before you count it.

The second blind spot: crawlers wearing a normal Chrome UA

The other failure mode is worse, because the UA looks perfect. I had a stream of Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X Safari UAs from 17.166.* — roughly two requests per page, and 159 distinct IPs in a single day. Nothing in the UA string says "bot".

The behaviour does:

  • exactly two requests per page (HTML + one asset), never the full asset set
  • no referrer, ever, and no session continuity
  • 159 IPs, all on the same cloud range, all doing the same thing within hours
  • zero interaction — no search query, no second page view, no scroll-triggered event

That's the profile of a distributed fetcher, not of people. Two requests per page means "I parsed your HTML", not "I read your page".

Here's the uncomfortable part: rendering completeness is not a reliable human signal any more. Googlebot loads CSS, executes JS, and would happily pass a "did they load the assets" check. I used to treat "loaded everything" as proof of humanity. It isn't. It only rules out the lazy crawlers.

What actually worked: four layers, in this order

  1. Classify at write time, store the verdict. A dev column (bot / tb / mb / pc) written by the Worker. Doing this at query time means every new bot name invalidates three months of history.
  2. Named crawlers get IP verification, not just UA matching. Google publishes its ranges; match 66.249., 64.233., 72.14., 74.125., 209.85. alongside the UA. This also removes the impostors: I had a bingbot UA from 209.112.91.75, which is a vulnerability scanner, not Bing. Real Bing crawls from 40.77.167., 52.167.144., 207.46.13., 157.55.39..
  3. Consistency checks on the claim. WeChat version vs build number vs IP ownership. Datacenter IP claiming to be a phone is a bot, no matter what the UA says.
  4. Request-shape checks for the rest. Assets loaded, referrer present, page-depth, inter-request timing. Any one alone is weak; three together are decisive.

Then every downstream number gets a single filter:

SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT ip) AS humans, COUNT(*) AS hits
FROM hits
WHERE COALESCE(dev, '') <> 'bot'
  AND date(ts, '+8 hours') = date('now', '+8 hours');

That COALESCE(dev, '') <> 'bot' has to be in every query — dashboard, admin panel, the JSON endpoint the frontend calls. I missed it in two places and got a "traffic surged" alert about my own crawler.

One more trap in the same query: my timestamps are stored in UTC. Comparing "today so far" against "yesterday's full day" made the dashboard report -93% on a completely normal morning. Six visits by 11:35 versus thirty-eight across the whole previous day isn't a decline, it's arithmetic. If your period comparison can produce a number that large, the bug is in the comparison, not the site.

What the honest number looks like

After filtering, on a 380-page site with 168 bilingual calculators:

Metric Before After
Best-day unique visitors 87 6
Traffic source "growing" 1 real organic click
Crawl coverage (Googlebot) unknown 372 / 380 pages
Crawl coverage (bingbot) unknown 5 / 380 pages

The last row is the one that changed my priorities. With bots stripped out, I could finally see that Google was indexing aggressively and Bing essentially wasn't crawling at all — a fact completely invisible in the inflated dashboard, where both were just "traffic".

You can't diagnose a funnel you can't measure. My dashboard was measuring machine labour and calling it demand.

Takeaway

If your analytics are hand-rolled, assume they're counting crawlers until you've proven otherwise. The cheap version of the proof:

  1. Log the UA and IP at write time — you can't retroactively classify what you didn't record.
  2. Treat every UA as a claim, then check it against IP ownership and request shape.
  3. Add <> 'bot' to every query, not just the pretty one.
  4. Compare like periods, in the same timezone, or your percentages will lie to you.

The site in question is jianzhujisuan.com — 168 construction-material calculators, 380 static pages, no framework. If you want to see what the crawling looks like from the other side, pick a page and view source; the result table is already in the HTML, which is why crawlers execute it and why my visitor count was fiction for three weeks.
